Genesis 31:38 has Jacob defend his years of service by noting that his ewes and goats had not miscarried. Leviticus 5:6 provides that a sin offering may be a female lamb or goat from the flock, showing ewes as acceptable offerings. Genesis 21:28 describes Abraham setting seven ewe lambs apart, a detail that became part of the story of the covenant at Beersheba.

ewe.etymology: From Middle English *ewe*, from Old English *eowu*, from **awi*, from Proto-Germanic **awiz*, from Proto-Indo-European **h₂ówis* (“sheep”).

senses.definition: Signifies agreement or recognition.
senses.example: So you're saying that we have only three days left? — Yes, exactly!

senses.definition: Of a manner, without approximation; precisely.
senses.example: Measure exactly so we can be sure it is right.

senses.definition: Of a focus, precisely, used to provide emphasis.
senses.example: He did it that way exactly to prove the point.

core.definition: Used to say you completely agree with someone or that something is exactly as they said.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, ZAKT. In casual American speech the t is often clipped, so it sounds close to ig-ZAK-lee.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It signals agreement and understanding, and it sounds warm and engaged in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Exactly!' often in casual talk and in meetings to show agreement or to confirm a point. A natural reply is simply 'Right' or 'Yeah, that's it.' Tone matters: a flat 'Exactly' can sound dismissive, so say it with some energy.

distinctions.note: Right is the most common all-purpose agreement word; exactly adds emphasis, meaning you agree fully.
Precisely is more formal and is used mostly in technical or careful speech; exactly is common in everyday talk.

examples.everyday: Neighbor: 'So the store closes at nine?' Me: 'Exactly, so we should hurry.'
examples.professional: Colleague: 'So we ship the fix on Friday regardless of the test results?' Me: 'Exactly, the deadline is fixed.'
examples.analytical: Exactly, the argument depends on whether the premise holds in every case, not just in the examples given.

nuance.analogy: It works like a key turning in a lock: it clicks into place and confirms the match.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exactus, past participle of exigere 'to drive out, finish, measure exactly'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'exactly' when you only partly agree; use 'sort of' or 'not exactly' instead.
Pronouncing the middle as two separate syllables, which makes it sound stiff.

conversation.text: "So we should leave early to beat traffic?" "Exactly."
"You mean the guy with the red hat?" "Exactly, that's him."
We got there at exactly six o'clock.

senses.definition: Very tired; zonked (out).
senses.example: The exhausted man fell asleep immediately.

senses.definition: Depleted of resources.
senses.example: The exhausted mine was worthless once all the ore had been extracted.

core.definition: Extremely tired, with no energy left, or having used up all of a supply.

pronunciation.tip: Stress ZAWS. The final -ed is pronounced as id, a separate syllable, because the word ends in t. Many non-native speakers drop the ending, which makes it sound like a different word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Used about people, it describes a state that is often sympathetic, though it can sound dramatic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I'm exhausted to mean very tired, especially after work, travel, or a long day. It is standard in everyday speech and writing. Informally, people may say I'm wiped or I'm beat, and a friend might reply oh no, get some rest.

distinctions.note: Tired is the everyday word for needing rest; exhausted is stronger and suggests you have no energy left at all.
Exhausted describes how you feel; exhausting describes the thing that makes you feel that way, like an exhausting trip.

examples.everyday: I'm so exhausted after the flight that I'm going straight to bed.
examples.professional: The team is exhausted after three weeks of release crunch, so let's move the next sprint review to Tuesday.
examples.analytical: Many modern thinkers believe their theories are exhausted, meaning the old questions have been answered in every way available.

nuance.analogy: A phone at two percent battery: running on fumes.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of exhaust, from Latin exhaurire, to draw out.
common_mistakes: Using exhausted to mean exhausting: I was exhausted the movie is wrong, while the movie was exhausting is correct.
Dropping the final -ed sound, which changes the meaning to a different word.

conversation.text: I'm exhausted after that long flight.
She was exhausted from working double shifts all week.
"You look exhausted." "I am. The kids were up at five."

senses.definition: A playful greeting when you see someone unexpectedly.

core.definition: A playful greeting said when you unexpectedly run into someone you know somewhere, such as a store or a street.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FAN in fancy and MEET in meeting, and let 'meeting you' link into one smooth phrase. The final 'r' in 'here' is pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Positive and playful. It signals surprise and friendliness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this with a smile when they bump into an acquaintance in a grocery store, at a ballgame, or on the street. A natural reply is 'Right? What are the odds!' or 'Small world!' It is casual, so avoid it in serious or formal situations.

distinctions.note: This is more neutral and less playful. Fancy meeting you here adds a light, cheerful tone.
Small world comments on how connected people are. Fancy meeting you here focuses on the surprise of running into someone in this exact place.

examples.everyday: Oh, hey, Tom! Fancy meeting you here at the hardware store.
examples.professional: Fancy meeting you here at the conference, Priya. I didn't know you were speaking this year.
examples.analytical: 'Fancy meeting you here,' she said, and the line made a chance encounter sound more like a plot than a coincidence.

nuance.analogy: It is like a little wave of surprise: a friendly hello that treats a random meeting as a small delight.
common_mistakes: Using fancy to mean luxurious, as in 'a fancy restaurant', when the greeting means 'surprising'.
Saying 'Fancy to meet you here' instead of 'Fancy meeting you here'.

conversation.text: Well, fancy meeting you here! Do you shop at this store too?
"Fancy meeting you here!" "I know! I didn't think you ever came to the gym."
Fancy meeting you here. I thought you were still in Boston.

senses.definition: The unfair favoring of one person or group at the expense of another.

core.definition: Unfair preference shown to one person or group over others who deserve equal treatment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAY, with a lighter secondary stress on 'tiz.' The middle syllables are quick and reduced, so 'favoritism' sounds like 'FAY-vrih-tiz-um.' Note the ending is '-izm,' not '-ism.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes unfair treatment and usually implies a complaint or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'favoritism' in workplaces, schools, families, and politics, usually to complain or to point out a problem, as in 'There's favoritism in how the manager assigns projects.' It is serious, so avoid using it lightly. A natural follow-up is to say 'I think that's unfair' or ask for transparent criteria.

distinctions.note: Bias is a general tendency to think or judge in a certain way, while favoritism is the active, unfair treatment of a particular person or group.
Nepotism is favoritism shown specifically to relatives or close friends, usually in hiring or promotion.

examples.everyday: My sister says our mom shows favoritism toward the youngest, and it really bothers her.
examples.professional: We need clear criteria for promotions so that no one can claim favoritism.
examples.analytical: Favoritism undermines the moral claim that institutions treat persons as equals before the law.

nuance.analogy: Favoritism is like a teacher who hands out the best seats to only a few students, while the rest get stuck in the back.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'favorite' with the suffix '-ism.'
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'favouritism' in American writing.
Pronouncing the ending as '-ism' with a short 'i' rather than '-izm' with a long 'i' sound.

senses.definition: Of land, etc.: capable of growing abundant crops; productive.
Of one's imagination, etc.: active, productive, prolific.
Capable of reproducing; fecund, fruitful.
senses.example: Most women at the age of fifty are not fertile.

senses.definition: Capable of developing past the egg stage.
Not itself fissile, but able to be converted into a fissile material by irradiation in a reactor.
senses.example: There are two basic fertile materials: uranium-238 and thorium-232.

core.definition: Able to produce crops, plants, or offspring; also describing a mind or idea that generates many new ideas.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. Americans often pronounce the middle t as a flap, sounding like a soft 'd', and the final syllable is a reduced 'ul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests productivity, growth and abundance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fertile' for soil, land, and in discussions of people's ability to have children. It can also describe a creative mind, as in 'a fertile imagination.' In casual talk, Americans might say 'productive' or 'rich soil' instead. In medical settings, 'fertile' refers to the ability to conceive.

distinctions.note: Productive is more general and common in work settings, while fertile is used for land, minds or biological ability.
Fruitful often describes results or outcomes, while fertile describes the source or ability to produce.

examples.everyday: That valley has really fertile soil, so the farmers grow corn and tomatoes there.
examples.professional: The brainstorming session was fertile, and we came away with three strong product ideas.
examples.analytical: The essay treats the period as fertile ground for new theological debates about grace and human freedom.

nuance.analogy: Fertile soil is like a garden bed that is ready for seeds to grow into many plants.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fertilis, from ferre, 'to bear, produce'.
common_mistakes: Using 'fertile' for a person's ideas in a way that sounds odd; say 'fertile mind' or 'productive mind' appropriately.
Mixing up 'fertile' and 'fertilize'; the first is an adjective, the second is a verb.

fertile.etymology: From Middle English, from Middle French *fertile*, from Old French *fertile*, from Latin *fertilis* (“fruitful, fertile”), from *ferō* (“to bear, carry”).

senses.definition: A small wooden vessel or cask of indeterminate size, used for butter, lard, etc.
A measurement for the mass of butter, equaling 56 pounds.

core.definition: A small wooden barrel or cask, traditionally used to store butter, lard, or ale.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ir' sound is the American r-colored vowel, like 'fur' in English, and the last syllable is a short, reduced 'in'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to an old container or measure, mostly in historical or literary writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use firkin today except in historical writing, cooking history, or old recipes and brewing history. Modern speakers would say 'barrel,' 'keg,' or 'tub.' If you see it in older texts, it generally means a small cask, and its exact size varied by goods and region.

distinctions.note: A barrel is the common modern word for a large cask; a firkin is a smaller, historical container.
A keg is a small metal or plastic container for beer today; a firkin is an older wooden vessel with a fixed historical sense.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's old recipe book mentions storing lard in a small firkin in the cellar.
examples.professional: The museum's exhibit on colonial trade listed each firkin of butter in its inventory.
examples.analytical: Historians of medieval commerce often rely on the firkin as a unit of measure, although its exact capacity varied by region.

nuance.analogy: A firkin is like an old-fashioned lunch pail: small, sturdy, and useful, but mostly seen in history books today.
nuance.etymology: From Middle Dutch 'vierdekijn' (fourth), meaning a quarter of a barrel, and related to Old English usage for a small cask.
common_mistakes: Assuming 'firkin' has a fixed modern size; its measure varied by product and place.
Pronouncing it 'FIR-kin' with a short 'i' in the first syllable instead of the r-colored 'ur' sound.
nuance.biblical_note: The word firkin is not used in the Revised Standard Version. Older English Bibles, such as the King James Version, use it in John 2:6 for the stone water jars at Cana, while the RSV describes those jars by their capacity in gallons. The Greek word behind this passage is metrētēs, a liquid measure of roughly 38 to 39 liters, and John 2:6 says each jar held two or three of these measures.

firkin.etymology: From Middle Dutch **vierdekijn*, diminutive of *vierde* (“fourth”), from *vier* (“four”); equivalent to *fourth* + *kin*.

senses.definition: An initial cause from which all other causes and effects follow.

core.definition: In philosophy and theology, an uncaused origin of all other causes and effects, often identified with God.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on CAUSE, the noun, while first is only secondary. In General American, cause rhymes with 'pause' in the cot-caught merger, so say KAHZ with an open ah vowel, not KAWZ with a rounded one.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in philosophy; reverent when used in theology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in philosophy classes, theology and debates about cosmology. In everyday talk people would say 'the origin of everything' or 'the beginning of it all.' In theological writing it often appears capitalized as First Cause.

distinctions.note: A root cause is the deepest cause of a problem in ordinary analysis; a first cause is metaphysical and names the origin of all causation.
Prime mover is Aristotle's term for an unmoved source of motion; first cause is broader and more often used in theistic arguments.

examples.everyday: My neighbor asked whether the universe needs a first cause, and we argued about it over coffee for an hour.
examples.professional: The incident report should name the root cause of the outage, not a first cause, so the fix prevents recurrence.
examples.analytical: Aquinas argued that a series of causes cannot regress infinitely, so there must be a first cause that is itself uncaused.

nuance.analogy: Like the first domino in a chain: it starts everything, yet no other domino pushed it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin prima causa, 'first cause'.
common_mistakes: Using first cause for root cause in ordinary problem solving, which is a different meaning
Treating it as casual everyday vocabulary when it is a technical philosophical term

senses.definition: To overwhelm with bewilderment; to amaze, confound, or stun, especially in a ludicrous manner.
senses.example: He was flabbergasted to find that his work had been done for him before he began.

senses.definition: An awkward person.
Overwhelming confusion, shock, or surprise.
senses.example: His flabbergast was so great he couldn’t even come up with a plausible answer.

core.definition: To shock or astonish someone so much that they are speechless or bewildered.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced 'er', and the final 'gast' rhymes with 'last'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to humorous. It describes strong surprise, usually a pleasant or funny kind.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flabbergast' in casual speech, often in the passive: 'I was flabbergasted when she told me.' It sounds lively and somewhat old-fashioned, so it is best with friends or family rather than in formal meetings. A common reply is 'No way!' or 'I can't believe it.'

distinctions.note: 'Astonish' is more neutral and formal; 'flabbergast' is more colorful and suggests a stronger shock.
'Surprise' is a general word; 'flabbergast' implies being thoroughly stunned, often speechless.

examples.everyday: I was flabbergasted when my neighbor told me he had run a marathon at seventy.
examples.professional: The client was flabbergasted by the forecast and asked us to explain the model again.
examples.analytical: The result was so unexpected that it flabbergasted even the researchers who had designed the study.

nuance.analogy: Like being hit with a sudden gust of wind that knocks you back a step, flabbergast leaves you momentarily stunned.
nuance.etymology: Probably a blend of 'flabby' and 'aghast', first recorded in the late 1700s.
common_mistakes: Using 'flabbergast' with 'of' or 'at'; the common forms are 'flabbergasted by' or 'flabbergasted at'.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel; it is reduced to 'er'.

flabbergast.etymology: The origin of the verb is; possibly dialectal, from *flabby* or *flap* (“to strike”) + *aghast* (for the latter, compare the variant spelling *flappergast*).

senses.definition: Likely to bend or break under pressure; easily damaged; frail, unsubstantial.
senses.example: He expected the flimsy structure to collapse at any moment.

senses.definition: Of clothing: very light and thin.
Of an argument, explanation, etc.: ill-founded, unconvincing, weak; also, unimportant; paltry, trivial.
senses.example: a flimsy excuse

senses.definition: Of a person: lacking depth of character or understanding; frivolous, superficial.
A thing which is ill-founded, unconvincing, or weak.
Thin typing paper used together with carbon paper in a typewriter to make multiple copies of a document; a sheet of such paper.
A document printed or typed on such paper.
A service certificate.
A banknote; paper money.
The text to be set into pages of magazines, newspapers, etc. copy.
To make (something) likely to be easily damaged.
To treat (someone or something) as paltry or unimportant; to demean, to underestimate.

(dated, historical) To type or write (text) on a flimsy (“sheet of thin typing paper used together with carbon paper in a typewriter to make multiple copies of a document”) (noun sense 2); to distribute such flimsies.
senses.label: dated, historical

core.definition: Easily damaged or broken; thin and weak, or unconvincing, as an argument or excuse.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FLIM. The final y is a long ee sound, so do not pronounce it as a short i.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes quality or reasoning as weak, and it is used both literally and figuratively.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for cheap furniture, clothing, or doors, and for excuses or arguments that do not hold up. Calling a plan flimsy in a meeting is a direct criticism, so soften it with phrases like a bit flimsy when talking to colleagues.

distinctions.note: Fragile means easily broken and needs careful handling, while flimsy means thin or poorly made and unconvincing.
Weak is a general term for lacking strength, while flimsy often suggests lightness or an argument that lacks support.

examples.everyday: That cheap plastic lawn chair feels too flimsy for my brother, so he bought a metal one.
examples.professional: The proposal's cost estimates look flimsy, so please add the source data before the review.
examples.analytical: Her claim about cultural decline rests on a flimsy comparison that ignores the historical record.

nuance.analogy: A flimsy argument is like a card house: it looks finished, but one breath knocks it down.
nuance.etymology: From a 17th-century dialect word, probably related to flimp, meaning to be limp or slack.
common_mistakes: Confusing flimsy with fragile when the object is delicate but not thin.
Saying more flimsy instead of the usual comparative form for a rare case; use flimsier only in informal speech.

senses.definition: An enemy.
A unit of energy equal to 10 joules.

core.definition: An enemy, a person or group that opposes or wants to harm you.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a long o. It is a homophone of the adjective roe? No; it sounds like the word oh with an f, so keep the vowel clear and do not confuse it with for.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests opposition, conflict or danger, and is stronger than rival or opponent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use foe in everyday conversation; they usually say enemy or opponent. Foe appears in literature, speeches, sports writing and headlines, and in phrases like friend or foe. In casual talk, saying my foe would sound dramatic, so use it for a serious or poetic moment.

distinctions.note: Enemy is the common everyday word for someone who wants to harm you, while foe sounds more literary or dramatic.
Opponent is neutral and used for a rival in a game, debate or election, while foe implies hostility.

examples.everyday: My old college roommate has become a real foe in our office politics, which is strange to say.
examples.professional: The competitor is a foe we respect, but our team plans to win the contract on the merits.
examples.analytical: The psalmist speaks of enemies and foes, and the poem's mood shifts from fear to confident trust in God.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess rival who wants to checkmate you, a foe is someone whose success means your defeat.
nuance.etymology: From Old English fāh, meaning hostile.
common_mistakes: Using foe in everyday talk, where enemy or opponent sounds more natural.
Confusing foe with for, which sounds the same as fore but is a different word.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, the common word for an enemy or foe is 'oyeb (אוֹיֵב), used for those who oppose the psalmist or the people of Israel. Psalm 18:17 says God rescued the psalmist from his strong enemy and from those who hated him. Psalm 27:2 describes evildoers and adversaries who attack the psalmist and whom God will make stumble.

foe.etymology: From Middle English *fo* (“foe; hostile”), from earlier *yfoh*, *yvo*, *ifa* (“foe”), from Old English *ġefāh* (“enemy”), from *fāh* (“hostile”), from **faih*, from Proto-Germanic **faihaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **peyḱ-* (“to hate, be hostile”).

senses.definition: At the moment.
senses.example: That's enough for now, we can continue our conversation tomorrow.

core.definition: At the present moment; for the time being, until something changes or is decided later.

pronunciation.tip: 'For' is weak and sounds like 'fer', so the stress falls on NOW. Keep the r in 'for' and avoid stretching the vowel into a diphthong too long.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals a temporary decision and can sound reassuring or mildly tentative depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'for now' constantly at work and in everyday life to close a conversation without finishing it, as in 'That's all for now.' It is equally natural in a meeting ('For now, let's keep the current schedule') or with friends ('Okay, see you tomorrow, that's all for now'). A natural reply is 'Sounds good' or 'Okay, talk later.'

distinctions.note: 'For the time being' is slightly more formal and emphasizes a longer pause, while 'for now' is more casual and conversational.
'Temporarily' is an adverb describing a state, while 'for now' is a phrase placed at the start or end of a sentence to mark a decision as provisional.

collocations: let's leave it at that for now

examples.everyday: The bathroom sink is fixed for now, but you should call a plumber next week.
examples.professional: For now, we'll keep the current deployment schedule and revisit it after the Q3 review.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'for now' marks a decision as provisional, so the claim it qualifies is held open rather than asserted as final.

nuance.analogy: It is like a parked car: it is not going anywhere yet, but it is not really moving either.
common_mistakes: Using 'for now' to mean 'currently' in a formal report where 'currently' is more precise.
Confusing 'for now' with 'for good', which means permanently.

conversation.text: Let's go with option A for now and revisit it next month.
For now, keep using the old system.
That's all I have for now. Thanks, everyone.

senses.definition: A sense of evil to come.
An evil omen.
Of ominous significance; serving as an ill omen; foretelling of harm or difficulty.

core.definition: A strong feeling or sense that something bad is going to happen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the final -ing is a short, reduced ending, so it sounds like 'for-BOH-ding'. Keep the r clear in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes an uneasy feeling that trouble is coming.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use foreboding as a noun for an uneasy, often unexplained feeling, as in 'I had a sense of foreboding before the meeting.' It is used in everyday speech and in writing. For a more casual feeling, people often say 'I had a bad feeling.' A natural reply is 'Me too' or 'Let's hope it's nothing.'

distinctions.note: A premonition can be good or bad and suggests a specific prediction, while foreboding is almost always a general, uneasy sense of trouble.
Dread is a strong emotion of fear about something coming; foreboding is more of a sense or intuition that something bad will happen.

examples.everyday: I had a sense of foreboding when the phone rang late at night, but it was just my sister with good news.
examples.professional: The team felt a growing foreboding as the server logs showed the same error every hour after deployment.
examples.analytical: Heidegger describes a foreboding about technology that is not a fear of a specific event but an uneasy sense of the way modern life frames everything.

nuance.analogy: Like the smell of rain before a storm: you cannot yet see the clouds, but you sense that something is coming.
nuance.etymology: From forebode, from fore, before, plus bode, from Old English bodian, to announce.
common_mistakes: Confusing foreboding with forbidding, which means threatening in appearance.
Using foreboding as a verb, as in 'I foreboding trouble', instead of the verb forebode.

senses.definition: The act of assembling a group or structure.
Something possessing structure or form.
The process during which something comes into being and gains its characteristics.
The process of influencing or guiding a person to a deeper understanding of a particular vocation.
A structure made of two categories, two functors from the first to the second category, and a transformation from one of the functors to the other.
A grouping of military units or smaller formations under a command, such as a brigade, division, wing, etc.
A layer of rock of common origin.
An arrangement of moving troops, ships, or aircraft, such as a wedge, line abreast, or echelon. Often "in formation".
An arrangement of players designed to facilitate certain plays.

core.definition: The process by which something develops, or the act of shaping or organizing a group or structure.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MAY, the second syllable. The first syllable is a weak fawr with a clear r, and the final syllable is a reduced shun, so do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is positive or neutral when describing growth or training, and can be neutral when describing an organized group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use formation for a group, like a team or military unit in formation, or for a process, like cloud formation or character formation. In church and faith settings, 'spiritual formation' is a common phrase. In everyday talk, people more often say 'how something came about' or 'how it started'.

distinctions.note: Formation is the process of forming something, while information is facts or data; the two are pronounced differently and not interchangeable.
Creation often implies bringing something new into existence, while formation stresses the developing shape or structure.

examples.everyday: The geese flew over the lake in a perfect V formation, and my son wanted to know how they learned it.
examples.professional: The formation of the new data team took about six months, mostly because of hiring delays.
examples.analytical: Augustine's account of the formation of the will treats desire as shaped over time by habit and grace.

nuance.analogy: Formation is like a riverbed being cut over years by water: the shape comes from a steady process, not one sudden act.
nuance.etymology: From Latin formatio, from formare, to shape, from forma, form.
common_mistakes: Confusing the pronunciation with 'information', which has a different stress and vowel in the second syllable.
Using 'formation' for a single decision; use 'decision' or 'choice' instead.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb morphoo means to form or shape, and Galatians 4:19 uses it for Christ being formed in believers. Romans 12:2 uses metamorphoo, to be transformed, for the renewal of the mind. Both passages describe spiritual formation as an ongoing change shaped by Christ rather than a single event.

formation.etymology: From Middle English *formacioun*, *formation*, borrowed from Old French *formacion*, from Latin *fōrmātiō*, from *fōrmō* (“form”); see form as verb.

senses.definition: Easily broken, not sturdy; of delicate material.
senses.example: She caught the fragile vase before it could shatter on the floor.

senses.definition: Readily disrupted or destroyed.
senses.example: The UN tries to maintain the fragile peace process in the region.

senses.definition: Something that is fragile.

core.definition: Easily broken or damaged; delicate and not strong, or in a weak or unstable condition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'g' before 'i' sounds like 'j' and the final 'le' is a light, unstressed 'uhl' with no full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, depending on context. It can describe a delicate object with care, or a weak emotional or economic state with concern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fragile' on packages ('Fragile: handle with care'), for objects, and for people's emotional states, often gently ('She's been fragile since the surgery'). Calling someone 'fragile' can sound condescending if said directly to them. In technical settings it describes systems that break under small changes.

distinctions.note: 'Delicate' stresses fineness or sensitivity and can be positive, as in delicate lace; 'fragile' stresses that something can break easily.
'Brittle' describes hard materials that snap rather than bend, and can describe a manner that seems hard but is not flexible.
'Weak' describes lack of strength in general; 'fragile' suggests a state that is easily damaged or broken.

examples.everyday: Be careful with that vase; it's really fragile.
examples.professional: The deployment pipeline is fragile, so any change to the config file can break the whole build.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on a fragile premise that collapses once we question the definition of consent.

nuance.analogy: A fragile system is like a house of cards: it stands fine until a small nudge brings it down.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fragilis, from frangere, 'to break.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel as a clear 'ah' rather than the short 'a' in 'fra'.
Using 'fragile' for people in a rude way; in American speech, 'sensitive' or 'going through a hard time' is often kinder.

fragile.etymology: Middle French *fragile*, from Latin *fragilis*, formed on frag, the root of *frangere* (“to break”).

senses.definition: In a fraudulent manner.

core.definition: In a dishonest way, by deceiving people in order to gain money or advantage.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FRAW, and the final -ly is a clear ee sound, not a separate syllable with a heavy stress. The -ently ending is usually reduced to a short uh and n sound, so the word has five syllables with a quick middle.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It always describes wrongdoing, usually in legal, financial, or official contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fraudulently mostly in news reports, legal writing, and business settings, for example, someone who fraudulently obtained benefits. In everyday speech people usually say they lied or cheated instead. It is a serious word, so use it only when you are describing deliberate deception.

distinctions.note: Illegally describes breaking the law in general, while fraudulently specifically describes deception used to gain something.
Dishonestly is a general word for not telling the truth or not acting honestly, and it is less legal in tone than fraudulently.

examples.everyday: The neighbor said that a man had fraudulently claimed to be a plumber and took money from her.
examples.professional: The auditor found that the manager had fraudulently recorded expenses that never happened.
examples.analytical: A contract signed under false pretenses was entered into fraudulently, so the court treated it as void.

nuance.analogy: Acting fraudulently is like a magician who hides the trick from you so you believe something false and hand over your money.
nuance.etymology: From fraudulent plus the adverb ending -ly, from Latin fraus, meaning deceit.
common_mistakes: Saying the middle syllable with a long o instead of the aw sound of FRAW.
Using fraudulently for a mistake; it requires intentional deception.
Dropping the -ly ending in speech so it sounds like an adjective.

senses.definition: Bearing no fruit; barren.
Unproductive, useless.
senses.example: The unskilled man’s attempt at fixing his car engine was fruitless.

senses.definition: (rare) Of a diet, etc.: without fruit.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Producing no useful result; unsuccessful and pointless despite effort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The ending is a weak 'lus' sound with a reduced vowel, not a full 'less.'

nuance.connotation: Negative: suggests effort that was wasted or did not work out.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fruitless when effort fails to produce results, like 'a fruitless search' or 'fruitless negotiations.' It works in both casual and formal speech and sounds softer than 'pointless,' which can sound rude. The literal sense about barren plants is less common in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Futile is stronger and more formal, suggesting nothing could succeed; fruitless often means one particular attempt failed.
Pointless is blunter and more casual, often implying the action had no purpose at all.

examples.everyday: We searched the whole mall for those boots, but it was fruitless.
examples.professional: After three fruitless vendor calls, we decided to build the integration in-house.
examples.analytical: Many debates about free will prove fruitless because the participants define the key terms differently from the start.

nuance.analogy: Like digging a well in dry ground: the work is real, but no water appears.
nuance.etymology: From fruit plus -less, meaning without fruit.
common_mistakes: Saying FROOT-less with a long e; the ending is a weak 'lus.'
Calling a person fruitless; for people, say unsuccessful or ineffective.

senses.definition: Of a thing: done with evasive or guilty secrecy.
Of a thing: that has been acquired by theft; stolen; also taken stealthily.
Of a person or an animal: sly, stealthy.
Of a person, etc.: inclined to steal; pilfering, thieving.

core.definition: Secretive and sneaky, done quietly to avoid being noticed, often because of guilt or fear of being caught.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a short, reduced vowel. Do not add a long 'ee' at the end; the final sound is a short 'iv'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it suggests guilty, secretive, or suspicious behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in writing, news, and descriptive speech when someone looks sneaky or hides something. In everyday conversation, people more often say 'sneaky' or 'secretive', so 'furtive' can sound a bit formal or literary. It is commonly used for glances, movements, or looks.

distinctions.note: Sneaky is casual and often means tricky or mischievous; furtive suggests a quiet, nervous attempt to avoid being seen.
Secretive describes a general habit of keeping things hidden; furtive describes a specific, nervous action in the moment.

examples.everyday: He gave me a furtive look and then hid the cookie jar behind his back.
examples.professional: The auditor noticed a furtive exchange of files between two staff members after the meeting.
examples.analytical: Dostoevsky's underground narrator often reveals a furtive shame that he cannot fully admit even to himself.

nuance.analogy: A furtive person is like a cat slipping past a room, quiet and careful not to be noticed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'furtivus' (stolen, secret), from 'furtum' (theft), from 'fur' (thief).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long 'ee' at the end, as in 'FUR-teev'.
Confusing it with 'furtive' meaning 'stolen', which is a rare, older sense.

furtive.etymology: From Middle English **furtyve* (implied in *furtyvely*), from Middle French *furtif*, *furtive* (“furtive, stealthy”), from Latin *fūrtīvus* (“clandestine, furtive, secret; concealed, hidden; stolen”), from *fūrtum* (“theft; robbery”) (from *fūr*…

senses.definition: In wireless internet, an access point with additional software capabilities such as providing NAT and DHCP, which may also provide VPN support, roaming, firewalls, various levels of security, etc.
A passage that can be closed by use of a gate.
A place regarded as giving access to somewhere.
Any point that represents the beginning of a transition from one place or phase to another.
senses.example: a gateway drug

senses.definition: Any thing or area of interest that tends to lead to deeper involvement.
senses.example: a gateway drug

senses.definition: A point at which freight moving from one territory to another is interchanged between transportation lines.
To make available using a gateway, or access point.

core.definition: A device or software that connects two networks or systems and translates between them, letting data pass through a controlled point.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GATE, and the second syllable, way, is unstressed in compounds like this one in American speech. Keep the t clear and avoid adding a vowel between gate and way.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In technical contexts it is purely descriptive; in general use it can be positive, as in a gateway to a career.
nuance.usage_note: In American tech conversation, gateway usually refers to a network device, such as a home router or a cloud API gateway, that connects one network to another. Outside tech, Americans also say gateway for something that leads to a larger opportunity, such as a community college being a gateway to a degree. The verb form is more common in engineering and product documentation.

distinctions.note: A router forwards packets within and between networks, while a gateway can also translate protocols and connect very different systems.
A portal is a single page or site that presents many services to users, while a gateway is a technical access point that controls traffic.

examples.everyday: My internet is slow, so the technician said the gateway in the closet needs a reset.
examples.professional: We route all external requests through an API gateway so we can enforce authentication and rate limits.
examples.analytical: Language is often treated as a gateway to culture, yet it can also become a barrier that filters what a community can see.

nuance.analogy: A gateway is like a customs checkpoint: it inspects what passes between two countries and speaks both languages.
nuance.etymology: From gate plus way, a passage through a gate.
common_mistakes: Confusing gateway with a simple gate, since the technical sense means a translating device.
Stressing the second syllable, as in gate-WAY.

senses.definition: The shortest curve between two points on a specific surface.
A segment of a great circle.
A course allowing the parallel-transport of vectors along a course that causes tangent vectors to remain tangent vectors throughout that course (a straight curve, a line that is straight).
Of or relating to geodesy.
Of or relating to a geodesic dome.

core.definition: Of or relating to geodesy, or to the shortest path between two points on a curved surface such as a sphere.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second-to-last syllable, DES, so keep the first syllables light and do not say GEE-o-desk. Pronounce the middle vowel as a quick schwa, not a full ah.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use geodesic mostly in mathematics, physics, surveying and engineering, and it is not everyday vocabulary. The noun form is also used for the path itself. In popular speech, geodesic dome is the most familiar phrase, and a geodesic dome is often seen at outdoor science centers and camps.

distinctions.note: Geodetic describes the science of measuring the earth's shape, while geodesic describes a shortest path on a curved surface. People often mix them up, but they are not interchangeable.
A great circle is a specific kind of geodesic on a sphere, formed by a plane through the center. All great circles are geodesics, but many geodesics on other surfaces are not great circles.

examples.everyday: The flight from Seattle to Madrid goes over Greenland because it follows a geodesic route across the globe.
examples.professional: Our GIS pipeline computes the geodesic distance between store locations on the WGS84 ellipsoid instead of using straight-line math.
examples.analytical: On a sphere, every geodesic is a segment of a great circle, and Gauss showed that this curvature property is intrinsic to the surface.

nuance.analogy: A geodesic on a curved surface is like a string pulled tight over a ball, which always takes the straightest possible route.
nuance.etymology: From French géodésique, from Greek geōdaisia, meaning division of land.
common_mistakes: Saying the stress on the first syllable, as in GEE-oh-dess-ik, instead of stressing DES.
Using geodesic when you mean geodetic, which refers to the science of measuring the earth.

senses.definition: To affect adversely; to upset or annoy.
senses.example: This job’s really getting to me. I don’t know how much longer I’ll last.

senses.definition: To reach or arrive at (a physical or abstract destination, or state of doing a certain activity).
senses.example: I’ll call you when I get to the railway station.

senses.definition: To go to or be located at (a particular place).
senses.example: Where has Jane got to? She was here just a moment ago.

senses.definition: To be allowed to.
senses.example: You won't get to have any dessert until you finish your vegetables.

senses.definition: To attack, intimidate or kill; to corrupt or bribe.
senses.example: He’s refusing to testify. I think the Mob got to him.

senses.definition: To begin (something); to get around to doing (something).
senses.example: He got to his chores in the afternoon.

core.definition: To affect someone adversely; to upset, annoy or bother them, especially through repetition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GET, and 'to' weakens to 'tuh' in fast speech, so it sounds like 'GE-tuh'. Americans often say 'gets to me' with the t linked and flapped.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes something that wears down your patience or mood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'It really gets to me' or 'That noise is getting to her' in casual talk about irritations and stress. Use it with a person as the object. A natural reply is 'I know, it's frustrating' or 'Yeah, it wears on you.'

distinctions.note: Bother is neutral and can be mild; get to often implies the irritation has built up over time.
Upset suggests strong emotional distress, while get to can describe a gradual wearing down of patience.

collocations: That noise is getting to her
It's starting to get to everyone
Don't let it get to you
Long hours get to people after a while

examples.everyday: Honestly, the construction noise outside my apartment is really getting to me.
examples.professional: The constant last-minute changes to the sprint scope are starting to get to the team.
examples.analytical: Small, repeated frustrations can slowly get to even the most patient researcher, distorting judgment over time.

nuance.analogy: Like water dripping on a stone: no single drop breaks it, but the repetition eventually wears it down.
common_mistakes: Saying 'It gets to me' when you mean 'I am able to reach it'; context matters, so use 'gets to me' only for irritation.
Using 'get to' with a thing as the object when you mean a person; it usually needs a person as the one affected.

conversation.text: Don't let his comments get to you.
The constant noise is really starting to get to me.
I finally got to see the Grand Canyon last summer.
What time did you get to the party?

senses.definition: To look or stare with anger.
An angry glare or stare.
senses.example: She sure has an awful glower on her face.

senses.definition: That which glows or emits light.

core.definition: To look at someone with an angry, sullen, or threatening expression.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is the reduced American 'er' sound. The 'ow' is a diphthong like 'cow,' so it is GLOW-er, not glow-ER.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests anger, resentment, or a sullen mood, and it usually describes a stare or facial expression rather than an open argument.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use glower mostly in storytelling and written descriptions, as in 'he glowered at the referee.' In everyday speech, people more often say 'glare' or 'give someone a dirty look.' Glower is vivid and slightly literary, so it works well in writing but may sound stiff in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Glare is the everyday word for an angry stare; glower is more literary and suggests a darker, more brooding anger.
A scowl involves a frown on the face; glower focuses more on the intensity of the eyes and the sullen mood.

examples.everyday: My little brother glowered at me when I took the last slice of pizza.
examples.professional: When the vendor missed the deadline again, the director glowered at the screen but said nothing in the meeting.
examples.analytical: The narrator's account of the old king, who glowers at his heirs, shows a ruler whose anger replaces political reasoning.

nuance.analogy: Like a storm cloud that hangs over a field: the anger is quiet but heavy and visible to everyone.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; possibly related to Middle English gloren, to stare.
common_mistakes: Confusing glower with glow, which means to shine softly
Using glower for a brief look, when it suggests a longer and more intense stare

glower.etymology: From an alteration of *glore*, from Middle English *gloren*, *glouren* (“to gleam; to glare, glower”); or from *glow* (“to stare”) obsolete, and ultimately from a Scandinavian language.

senses.definition: A person who makes, repairs or sells things of gold, especially jewelry.

core.definition: A person who makes, repairs or sells objects of gold, especially jewelry.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final th is voiceless, like the th in think, and the cluster ldsm is pronounced without inserting a vowel between l, d and s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests skill, craft and fine work with precious metal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use goldsmith for a craftsperson who works with gold, and it is somewhat less common than jeweler in everyday speech. A jeweler may sell and set stones, while a goldsmith works with metal. In casual talk people often say jeweler for both.

distinctions.note: A jeweler sells and often repairs jewelry, possibly setting stones; a goldsmith mainly makes and works the gold itself.
A silversmith works in silver rather than gold, using similar hand-working methods.

examples.everyday: My aunt took her old ring to a goldsmith downtown to have it resized.
examples.professional: The museum commissioned a goldsmith to restore the ceremonial cup.
examples.analytical: In the ancient world the goldsmith was often a religious craftsman as well, since gold objects were used in temples.

nuance.analogy: A goldsmith is like a sculptor who works in a metal that never tarnishes: the craft is in shaping and joining the precious material.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gold and smith, from Old English smith, a metalworker.
common_mistakes: Using goldsmith for any jewelry shop; many jewelers do not make the metal objects themselves.
Pronouncing the final th as a t or d.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word tsorep refers to a metalworker who refines and shapes gold and silver. In Isaiah 40:19 a craftsman casts an idol and a goldsmith overlays it with gold, mocking the making of images. Isaiah 46:6 gives a similar picture of people paying a goldsmith to make an idol. In Nehemiah 3:8 a goldsmith named Uzziel helps repair the wall of Jerusalem, showing skilled craftsmen serving the restoration.

goldsmith.etymology: From Middle English *goldsmith*, from Old English *goldsmiþ* (“goldsmith”), from Proto-Germanic **gulþasmiþaz* (“goldsmith”), equivalent to *gold* + *smith*.

senses.definition: To please.
To make content; to satisfy.
senses.example: gratify the critics

core.definition: To please someone or satisfy a want, feeling or desire, often in a formal or polite way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final 'ify' ends with a clear 'fye' sound, rhymed with 'by'. The middle syllable is reduced to a short 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it suggests pleasing someone, though it can imply catering to desire.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gratify in formal speech and writing, such as 'I'm gratified to hear that'. In casual talk they usually say 'I'm glad' or 'That makes me happy'. It is often used to express satisfaction at good news in business or public settings.

distinctions.note: Please is the everyday word for making someone happy, while gratify is more formal and often suggests satisfying a desire or expectation.
Satisfy is broader and common, while gratify emphasizes pleasing or rewarding someone.

examples.everyday: I'm gratified that the restaurant still remembers my order after all these years.
examples.professional: We are gratified by the strong response to the pilot program and look forward to expanding it.
examples.analytical: The argument does not gratify the reader's appetite for certainty, which is precisely its strength.

nuance.analogy: To gratify someone is like handing them the exact thing they hoped for, so their face relaxes into a smile.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'gratificari', to do a favor, from 'gratus' meaning pleasing and 'facere' meaning to make.
common_mistakes: Using 'gratify' for everyday happiness, which can sound stiff in casual talk.
Confusing gratify with gratifying, the adjective used for things that are pleasing.

gratify.etymology: From French *gratifier*, from Latin *grātificō* (“to do a favor to, oblige, please, gratify”), from *grātus* (“kind, pleasing”) + *faciō* (“to make”).

senses.definition: A selfish or excessive desire for more than is needed or deserved, especially of money, wealth, food, or other possessions.
senses.example: His greed was his undoing.

senses.definition: To desire in a greedy manner, or to act on such a desire.
To play greedily or aggressively in a high-risk, high-reward scenario.

core.definition: A strong, selfish desire for more money, possessions, power, or food than one needs or deserves.

pronunciation.tip: Greed has one syllable with a long ee sound. Keep the d clear at the end, and do not turn the vowel into a short i as in grid.

nuance.connotation: Negative, an accusation of selfishness; used in politics, economics and moral discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use greed in political speeches, news stories and everyday criticism of selfish behavior. Calling someone greedy is a strong insult, so say it carefully. It is often paired with words like corporate or pure, and in moral contexts Americans often mention greed as one of the seven deadly sins.

distinctions.note: Ambition is a drive to achieve or succeed and can be admirable; greed is a selfish desire for more than is needed or deserved.
Desire is a neutral wish for something; greed is an excessive, selfish form of desire.

examples.everyday: My neighbor thinks the developers are just driven by greed and do not care about the park.
examples.professional: The board rejected the proposal because it looked like a short-term grab driven by greed rather than a long-term investment.
examples.analytical: Aquinas treats greed as a form of avarice that disorders the right ordering of goods, so the problem lies in the will rather than in possessions themselves.

nuance.analogy: Greed is like a fire that is fed by what it consumes: the more it gets, the hungrier it becomes.
nuance.etymology: From Old English graedig, related to greedy; the noun developed from the adjective.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like grid with a short i; the vowel is long ee.
Using greed as a countable noun in the plural, as in greeds; it is normally uncountable.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word pleonexia, often translated covetousness or greed, means a desire to have more. Luke 12:15 warns against all covetousness, saying that a person's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. Ephesians 5:5 calls the covetous person an idolater, and Colossians 3:5 links covetousness with idolatry.

core.definition: Mother of the prophet Samuel. She prayed desperately at Shiloh for a son, then dedicated him to serve the Lord, and she is remembered as a model of faithful prayer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final vowel is a soft, reduced uh sound, not a long ah. Don't pronounce the h in the middle as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; in religious settings it recalls prayer, faithfulness and gratitude.
nuance.usage_note: Hannah is a common given name in the United States, and it is also used in religious contexts when people discuss the Bible. When talking about the biblical figure, Americans usually say the Hannah of 1 Samuel or Hannah's prayer. Her story often comes up in sermons and Bible studies about prayer and dedication.

distinctions.note: Anna is a different prophetess in the New Testament (Luke 2:36), not the mother of Samuel; the two names are sometimes confused.

collocations: Hannah dedicated Samuel to the Lord

examples.everyday: My friend Sarah named her daughter Hannah after her grandmother.
examples.professional: In the sermon series on prayer, our pastor used Hannah's story to explain persistent prayer.
examples.analytical: Hannah's prayer in 1 Samuel 1 moves from grief to vow, showing how lament can become thanksgiving.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Channah, from a root meaning grace or favor.
common_mistakes: Saying HUH-nah instead of HAN-uh
Confusing her with the New Testament prophetess Anna
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Channah (Ḥannāh), from hen, meaning grace or favor. 1 Samuel 1:10-11 describes her bitter weeping and her vow to give a son to the Lord if he would grant one. 1 Samuel 1:27-28 tells how she gave Samuel to the service of the Lord after he was born. 1 Samuel 2:1-10 records her song of thanksgiving, which celebrates God's power to lift up the lowly.

hannah.etymology: From previous romanizations of Hebrew *חַנָּה*, chiefly for the mother of Samuel, from *חַנָּה* (“grace, gracious, graced with child”).

senses.definition: A person or thing that foreshadows or foretells the coming of someone or something.
senses.example: harbinger of danger; harbinger of doom; harbinger of spring

senses.definition: To announce or precede; to be a harbinger of.

core.definition: Noun: a sign or person that signals something is about to happen. Verb: to signal or announce that something will happen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is short and quick, and the final syllable is the American er sound, not a separate 'ur' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It often refers to a sign of something coming, sometimes something unpleasant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use harbinger in writing, news analysis and formal speech, usually for something important such as a trend or change. It sounds bookish in casual talk. A natural everyday alternative is 'sign' or 'warning sign'.

distinctions.note: Sign is common and neutral. Harbinger is more formal and suggests something important is about to arrive.
An omen is a sign, often supernatural, of what will happen. A harbinger can be an ordinary event that announces a change.

collocations: a harbinger of things to come

examples.everyday: That first cold snap was a harbinger of a rough winter, my neighbor said.
examples.professional: The sharp rise in support tickets is a harbinger of a larger problem in the new release.
examples.analytical: For the prophets, famine and war were harbingers of God's judgment, signs calling Israel to repentance.

nuance.analogy: A harbinger is like the first robin in spring: it arrives before the season is fully here and tells you the change is coming.
nuance.etymology: From Old French herbergere, 'one who provides lodging', from herberge, 'shelter', from Old High German heriberga.
common_mistakes: Using harbinger for a person who simply brings a message; it means a sign or forerunner.
Stressing the second syllable, which is a common mistake for learners.

harbinger.etymology: Originally, a person sent in advance to arrange lodgings.

senses.definition: To become hard.
To make something hard or harder.
To strengthen.
To modify (a website or other system) to make it resistant to malicious attacks.
To become or make (a person or thing) resistant or less sensitive.
To get an erection.
To become or make (a consonant) more fortis; to (cause to) undergo fortition.
To unpalatalize or velarize.

core.definition: To become hard or make something hard; in the Bible, to become stubborn and refuse to listen, especially to God.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable has no vowel: the d goes straight into a syllabic n, with the tongue staying on the ridge. Pronounce the r clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for physical change; negative when it describes hearts or attitudes becoming cold or stubborn.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'harden' for physical things (concrete, arteries) and for hearts, attitudes, or positions. 'Harden your heart' is a biblical phrase used in sermons. In security, 'harden a system' means to make it more resistant to attack.

distinctions.note: Toughen suggests becoming stronger or more resilient; harden often suggests rigidity or coldness.
Stiffen means to become less flexible, often temporarily or from fear or cold.
Solidify means to change from liquid or soft to solid, or to make a position firm.

examples.everyday: Let the glue harden for an hour before you move the shelf.
examples.professional: Our security team will harden the servers before we go live.
examples.analytical: In Exodus, the language of Pharaoh's hardening raises the question of how divine sovereignty relates to human responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Like clay left in the sun, a heart that keeps refusing to listen slowly sets.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English hardnen, from Old English heard, 'hard', plus -en.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing a vowel before the n: 'HAR-den' with a full e.
Using 'harden' for becoming strong in a positive sense where 'toughen' or 'strengthen' sounds more natural.
Dropping the r.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew verbs chazaq (to be strong, make firm), kaved (to make heavy) and qashah (to make hard) describe hardening of the heart. In Exodus 7:3 God says he will harden Pharaoh's heart, while in Exodus 8:15 Pharaoh hardens his own heart. Psalm 95:8 warns people not to harden their hearts as at Meribah. Hebrews 3:7-8 quotes this warning, using Greek sklerynō, 'to make hard'.

senses.definition: To leave, depart; to go on ahead.
senses.example: Alright, I'm going to head out

core.definition: To leave a place and begin going somewhere, often on a trip or errand.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'out' strongly. The vowel in 'out' is a diphthong; don't reduce it to 'oot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and casual: it signals leaving for a planned trip, outing, or errand.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'head out' when they are about to leave for an outing, a hike, a road trip, or an errand, as in 'We're heading out to the lake at ten.' It is casual and common in spoken English. A natural reply is 'Have fun' or 'Be safe out there.'

distinctions.note: 'Leave' is neutral and general; 'head out' is casual and often suggests setting off on a trip or activity.
'Head home' names the destination, while 'head out' does not say where you are going.

examples.everyday: We're heading out to the lake, so call me if you need anything.
examples.professional: Once the training is done, a few of us will head out to the client site for the afternoon.
examples.analytical: Rather than remain in the library, the researchers chose to head out into the field to test the claim directly.

nuance.analogy: Heading out is like opening a door and stepping onto the porch: you have left the room and you are now on your way.
nuance.etymology: 'Head' (from Old English heafod) plus 'out' (from Old English ūt), combining direction with departure.
common_mistakes: Saying 'head out from' with an unnecessary preposition when the place is already clear.
Confusing 'head out' with 'head off', which can mean leaving or stopping someone.

conversation.text: I'm going to head out now, see you tomorrow.
We headed out early to beat the traffic.
We head out for the airport at six.
What time do you want to head out tomorrow?
I'm about to head out. Do you need anything from the store?
It's getting late. I think I'm going to head out.

core.definition: A valley south of Jerusalem, called the Valley of Hinnom, which in the Bible became associated with child sacrifice and later with the image of hell.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced 'um'. Do not pronounce the final 'm' as a separate vowel or stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Hinnom mainly in Bible study, theology, archaeology and history, often in the phrase 'Valley of Hinnom'. In everyday conversation people usually would not mention it, but in church or a seminary setting it is a normal name.

distinctions.note: Hinnom is the valley's name, while Gehenna is the Greek form used in the New Testament for a place of punishment associated with it.

collocations: the valley of the son of Hinnom

examples.everyday: When we visited Jerusalem, our guide pointed toward the Valley of Hinnom and told us its history.
examples.professional: In the seminary course, I covered the archaeology of the Valley of Hinnom and its connection to the tophet.
examples.analytical: The prophet Jeremiah's condemnation of child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom shapes the later New Testament usage of Gehenna.

nuance.analogy: Like a place whose name became a warning sign: people in later centuries heard Hinnom and thought of judgment.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Ge-Hinnom, meaning 'valley of Hinnom', probably named after a person.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable.
Confusing Hinnom with Hilkiah or Hinn, which are different names.
nuance.biblical_note: The Valley of Hinnom lies south of Jerusalem, and Joshua 15:8 uses it to describe the boundary of Judah. Jeremiah 7:31 condemns the high place of Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, where people burned their sons and daughters, and in the New Testament the Greek Gehenna is derived from this place.

senses.definition: White, whitish, or grayish-white.
White or gray with age.
senses.example: The old man bowed his hoary head in acquiescence.

senses.definition: Of a pale silvery gray.
Covered with short, dense, grayish white hairs.
Old or old-fashioned; trite.

core.definition: White or gray with age, or old and respected because of long experience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HOR, and the second syllable is a light 'ee.' Learners often stress the second syllable or say it as two equal syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing age and wisdom; slightly negative when describing an old joke or cliché.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hoary' mainly in writing or formal speech, for example about a hoary tradition or hoary joke. In everyday talk they would say 'gray' or 'old.' Calling a joke 'hoary' suggests it is so old it is no longer funny.

distinctions.note: 'Gray' is the everyday color word; 'hoary' is literary and suggests age, frost, or long history.
'Ancient' refers to great age in time; 'hoary' adds the idea of respect or staleness.

examples.everyday: Grandpa told that hoary joke again, the one about the horse and the bar.
examples.professional: Our manager keeps bringing up the hoary idea that we should just work harder.
examples.analytical: The hoary debate between faith and reason still shapes how theologians introduce their arguments.

nuance.analogy: Like frost on a winter field, hoary describes a surface that has turned pale and old.
nuance.etymology: From 'hoar' (white or gray with age) plus the suffix '-y.'
common_mistakes: Using 'hoary' for a person's hair in everyday speech, where 'gray' is more natural.
Stressing the second syllable as in 'HOR-EE' with equal emphasis; keep the stress on the first syllable.

hoary.etymology: Possibly from Middle English **hori* (suggested by *horilocket* (“hoary-locked, having hoary locks or curls”)), equivalent to *hoar* + *y*.

core.definition: A Levite in the post-exilic period who helped Ezra explain the Law to the people in Jerusalem.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the final syllable is a light 'uh'. Americans say the 'o' as a long 'oh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a biblical name used in religious study.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches and Bible classes, Hodiah is mainly known from careful study of Nehemiah. Most people would not use the name in conversation, but a pastor or seminary student might mention him when discussing the Levites.

distinctions.note: Hodijah is a variant spelling found in some Bible translations for the same or a similar name.

examples.everyday: I was reading Nehemiah with my study group, and we noticed Hodiah among the Levites who taught the people.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, I listed Hodiah as one of the Levites who helped the community understand the Law.
examples.analytical: The list of Levites in Nehemiah 8 includes Hodiah, whose role illustrates the shared work of teaching the Law after the exile.

nuance.analogy: Hodiah is like a minor character in a historical record whose name appears in a list but whose function matters for the story.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew personal name Hodhiyah, meaning 'majesty of Yah' or similar; the exact meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'HOH-dye-uh'.
Confusing him with other Old Testament figures with similar names.
nuance.biblical_note: Hodiah (Hebrew Hodhiyah) was a Levite who, with other Levites, helped Ezra the scribe explain the Law to the people after the return from exile. Nehemiah 8:7 lists him among those who helped the people understand the reading of the Law. Nehemiah 10:10 mentions him again among the Levites who sealed the covenant. These passages show Levites as teachers of Scripture to the community.

senses.definition: The ingroup.
senses.example: Let's have a round of applause for the home team, as these quarterly production numbers are a big win.

senses.definition: The team that is playing in the usual area that they play in, as opposed to their opponents, the visiting team.
senses.example: The home team really pulled off a surprise in the bottom of the ninth. It made for some really exciting baseball for all these lucky fans out here today.

core.definition: The team that plays in its own home stadium or field, as opposed to the visiting team.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on 'team', and 'home' has a lighter stress. Keep the 'm' of 'home' and link it into 't' of 'team' for a smooth phrase.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests loyalty and local pride.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'home team' in sports conversation and at games, often with cheering. You might hear 'Let's root for the home team!' A natural reply is 'Go, team!' It is casual and friendly, and it can be used figuratively for a group in its own territory.

distinctions.note: The visiting team plays away; the home team plays in its own venue and usually has the crowd's support.
The host team hosts a tournament or event; the home team is the team that plays in its regular venue.

collocations: the home team takes the field

examples.everyday: We're cheering for the home team tonight, so wear your jersey!
examples.professional: Our product team is the home team for this launch, so the rest of the company should support their timeline.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the home team enjoys a measurable advantage in officiating decisions, which raises questions about fairness in sport.

nuance.analogy: Like a host at a party: the people in their own house have the familiar space and the friends in the room.
nuance.etymology: 'Home' from Old English ham; 'team' from Old English teme, 'offspring, line', later 'a group working together'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'house team' for the team that plays at home.
Using 'home team' for a company's headquarters team in a casual way without context.

conversation.text: The home team wears white tonight.
The crowd went crazy when the home team scored.
The home team usually has an advantage in the playoffs.

senses.definition: In any of several technical senses uniform; scalable; having its behavior or form determined by, or the same as, its behavior on or form at a smaller component (of its domain of definition, of itself, etc.).
senses.example: The polynomial x2+5xy+y2 is homogeneous of degree 2, because x2, xy, and y2 are all degree 2 monomials

senses.definition: Such that all its nonzero terms have the same degree.
senses.example: The polynomial x2+5xy+y2 is homogeneous of degree 2, because x2, xy, and y2 are all degree 2 monomials

senses.definition: Such that all the constant terms are zero.

Such that if each of f 's inputs are multiplied by the same scalar, f 's output is multiplied by the same scalar to some fixed power (called the degree of homogeneity or degree of f). Satisfying the equality f(s𝐱)=skf(𝐱) for some integer k and for all 𝐱 in the domain and s scalars.
senses.example: The function f(x,y)=x2+x2y+y2 is not homogeneous on all of ℝ2 because f(2,2)=16≠2k∗3=2kf(1,1) for any k, but f is homogeneous on the subspace of ℝ2 spanned by (1,0) because f(αx,αy)=αx2=α2f(x,y) for all (x,y)∈Span⁡{(1,0)}.

senses.definition: Informally: Everywhere the same, uniform, in the sense that any point can be moved to any other (via the group action) while respecting the structure of the space. Formally: Such that the group action is transitively and acts by automorphisms on the space (some authors also require that the action be faithful).
Of or relating to homogeneous coordinates.
Holding between a set and itself; being an endorelation.
Of the same kind; alike, similar.
Having the same composition throughout; of uniform make-up.
Of polynomials, functions, equations, systems of equations, or linear maps:
senses.example: The polynomial x2+5xy+y2 is homogeneous of degree 2, because x2, xy, and y2 are all degree 2 monomials

senses.definition: In ordinary differential equations (by analogy with the case for polynomial and functional homogeneity):
Capable of being written in the form f(x,y)dy=g(x,y)dx where f and g are homogeneous functions of the same degree as each other.
Having its degree-zero term equal to zero; admitting the trivial solution.
Homogeneous as a function of the dependent variable and its derivatives.
In abstract algebra and geometry:

Belonging to one of the summands of the grading (if the ring is graded over the natural numbers and the element is in the kth summand, it is said to be homogeneous of degree k; if the ring is graded over a commutative monoid I, and the element is an element of the ith summand, it is said to be of grade i)

Which respects the grading of its domain and codomain. Formally: Satisfying f(Vj)⊆Wi+j for fixed i (called the degree or grade of f), Vj the jth component of the grading of f 's domain, Wk the kth component of the grading of f 's codomain, and + representing the monoid operation in I.
In miscellaneous other senses:

Informally: Determined by its restriction to the unit sphere. Formally: Such that, for all real t>0 and test functions ϕ(𝐱), the equality S[t−nϕ(𝐱/t)]=tmS[ϕ(𝐱)] holds for some fixed real or complex m.
In the same state of matter.

core.definition: Uniform in composition or structure; in mathematics, having all terms of the same degree, or all parts behaving the same way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the JEE syllable, and the 'g' is a soft j sound. Keep the vowel in 'homo-' short and reduced, so it sounds like 'huh-muh' rather than 'HOM-oh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes uniformity without judging whether uniformity is good or bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use homogeneous in science, math, statistics and social science, and also in general speech about groups or mixtures that are uniform, like a homogeneous population. In casual talk people more often say 'all the same' or 'similar'. The word is common in academic and professional writing.

distinctions.note: The exact opposite: made of unlike parts or of different kinds.
Uniform stresses sameness of appearance or form, while homogeneous stresses sameness of composition or structure throughout.

examples.everyday: Our neighborhood is pretty homogeneous, so almost everyone here grew up in the same kind of town.
examples.professional: Before we pool the data, we need to confirm that the test samples are homogeneous across all three sites.
examples.analytical: A homogeneous polynomial is one in which every term has the same total degree, and this uniformity is what makes its scaling behavior so predictable.

nuance.analogy: A glass of skim milk looks the same in every spoonful, which is what homogeneous means.
nuance.etymology: From Greek homogenes, 'of the same kind', from homos 'same' and genos 'kind'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the stress: the stress is on JEE, not on HO or NEE-us.
Using homogeneous for a crowd of people who only look alike, when the word means uniform in composition or nature.

homogeneous.etymology: From Medieval Latin *homogeneus*, from Ancient Greek *ὁμογενής* (“of the same race, family or kind”), from *ὁμός* (“same”) + *γένος* (“kind”).

senses.definition: A brief meeting of all the players from one team that are on the field with the purpose of planning the following play.
A small group of individuals in very close proximity to one another.
A session in which a group of journalists assemble in an informal, dense cluster to question a person of interest.
A hesitation during play to think about one's next move.
To crowd together.
senses.example: The sheep huddled together seeking warmth.

senses.definition: To curl one's legs up to the chest and keep one's arms close to the torso; to crouch; to assume a position similar to that of an embryo in the womb.
To get together and discuss a topic.
To form a huddle.
To crowd (things) together; to mingle confusedly; to assemble without order or system.
To do, make, or put, in haste or roughly; hence, to do imperfectly; usually with a following preposition or adverb (huddle on, huddle up, huddle together).
To hesitate during play while thinking about one's next move.
Huddled, confused, congested.

core.definition: A brief, informal meeting or close gathering of a small group, often to talk privately or quickly plan what to do next.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, HUH. The second syllable is a reduced 'duhl,' with the 'l' sounding like a light, final 'l' rather than a separate vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests teamwork, quick coordination and a friendly, close group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'huddle' for sports teams planning a play, but also for quick workplace meetings: 'let's do a quick huddle.' It is informal and friendly, so it fits teams and small groups better than formal committees. Phrases like 'team huddle' and 'quick huddle' are common in offices.

distinctions.note: A 'meeting' is more formal and often scheduled; a 'huddle' is shorter, more informal and often spontaneous.
A 'conference' is large and formal; a 'huddle' is small, quick and close.

examples.everyday: Hang on, we're doing a quick huddle with the kids before we decide where to eat.
examples.professional: Let's do a quick huddle at 9:15 to decide who takes the customer call before the rollout.
examples.analytical: The team's short huddle before each sprint is a small ritual that aligns priorities without the formality of a full planning meeting.

nuance.analogy: Like a football team gathering in a tight circle between plays: a short, close conversation that sets the next move.
common_mistakes: Saying 'make a huddle'; Americans usually say 'have a huddle' or 'do a huddle.'
Using 'huddle' for a formal, scheduled meeting in a formal setting.

huddle.etymology: From Middle English **hudelen*, alteration (due to *hudels*, *hidels* (“hiding place”), see *hiddle*) of **huderen*, *hoderen* (“to cover; press together; huddle”), a frequentative form of Middle English *huden*, *hiden* (“to hide”), equivalent to *hide* +…

conversation.text: Let's have a quick huddle after lunch to plan the demo.
The team huddled for five minutes before the client call.
Can we huddle on this before you send the email?

senses.definition: Stating the reason for your call.

core.definition: A phrase that opens a phone call and states that the reason for your call is a purchase you already made.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'OR' in 'order' and on the first syllable of 'calling'. The 'r' in 'order' is strong and rhotic, so say 'OR-der' clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite. It states the reason briefly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this with online retailers, delivery services and utility companies. Give your order number if you have it, since this speeds things up. A natural reply is 'Sure, what's your order number?' It is more casual than 'I'm calling in reference to my order'.

distinctions.note: The same phrase; 'calling to check on my order' adds the purpose, which is more precise.

distinctions.vs: I'm calling to check on my order
distinctions.note: Adds a specific purpose; useful when you want a status update.

collocations: calling about my order from last week

examples.everyday: Hi, I'm calling about my order from last Tuesday, and it still hasn't shipped.
examples.professional: Hi, I'm calling about my order for the lab supplies, PO number 8812, because the invoice does not match.
examples.analytical: The caller's opening, 'I'm calling about my order', assumes a shared transaction the representative can look up and verify.
