nuance.analogy: It is like handing over a receipt before you explain the problem.
nuance.etymology: 'Order' comes from Latin ordo, row or rank, through Old French ordre.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I'm calling for my order' when you mean the topic; use 'about' here.
Mispronouncing 'order' as 'or-DER'; the stress falls on the first syllable.

conversation.text: Hi, I'm calling about my order. It hasn't arrived yet.
I'm calling about my order from last Tuesday; it's the wrong size.
"How can I help you?" "I'm calling about my order."

senses.definition: Creating new images with an AI model.

core.definition: The process of using an AI model to create new images from data, prompts, or other inputs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress IM in image and RAY in generation. The second syllable of generation is reduced to uh, so avoid saying 'jen-er-AY-shun' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in tech settings, but it can sound controversial when discussing artists or copyright.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use image generation for AI tools that create pictures from text prompts or other images. In casual talk, people often say 'AI art' or 'AI pictures,' but in work contexts image generation is the precise term. Be careful when discussing it with artists, since the topic can raise concerns about copyright.

distinctions.note: Image editing changes an existing image, while image generation creates a new image from scratch.
Image recognition identifies content in an image; image generation produces new visual content.

collocations: a generative model for image generation

examples.everyday: My daughter used an app that does image generation, and she made a picture of her dog as an astronaut.
examples.professional: Our marketing team wants to test image generation for product mockups, but legal needs to review the training data first.
examples.analytical: The essay asks whether image generation changes what counts as authorship when a model learns from millions of human artworks.

nuance.analogy: Image generation is like a painter who has studied a million paintings and can now paint a new one from a short description.
common_mistakes: Using 'generate images' in a sentence where Americans would normally say 'create images' in everyday speech.
Stressing the wrong syllable in generation, which is jen-uh-RAY-shun.

conversation.text: Image generation models create new images from a text description or another image.
Much modern image generation relies on diffusion models, which gradually turn random noise into a picture.
Marketing uses image generation for concept art, but final assets still go through a designer.

senses.definition: Existing only in the imagination.
senses.example: imaginary friend

senses.definition: Relating or belonging to the imagination.
Having no real part; that part of a complex number which is a multiple of −1 (called imaginary unit).
Imagination; fancy.
An imaginary number.
The set of values, institutions, laws, and symbols common to a particular social group and the corresponding society through which people imagine their social whole.

core.definition: Existing only in the mind or imagination, not in reality.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on MAJ, the second syllable. Don't pronounce the middle vowel as a long ee; it is a short ih, and the final -ary is often said as -ary or -ary-ee with a weak ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it can sound negative when describing a problem or fear that is not real.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use imaginary for things that are made up or exist only in the mind, as in 'an imaginary friend' or 'imaginary fears.' In math, the word has a precise technical meaning. In casual speech, say made up or pretend for playful contexts, but imaginary is natural and common.

distinctions.note: Imaginative describes a person or work that shows creativity; imaginary describes something that does not exist outside the mind.
Fictional usually describes stories or characters, while imaginary can describe fears, places, or friends in ordinary life.

examples.everyday: When I was little, I had an imaginary friend named Bob who lived under my bed.
examples.professional: The forecast model used an imaginary scenario to test what would happen if all clients left at once.
examples.analytical: Descartes treats some ideas as imaginary, meaning they depend on sensory images rather than clear reasoning.

nuance.analogy: An imaginary idea is like a drawing of a dragon: you can picture it clearly, but it does not walk outside.
nuance.etymology: From Latin imaginarius, relating to images, from imago, image.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable: it is ih-MAJ-ih-ner-ee.
Using imaginary to mean imaginative, which describes creative people or ideas.

imaginary.etymology: From Middle English *ymaginarie*, *ymagynary*, from Latin *imāginārius* (“relating to images, fancied”), from *imāgō*, equivalent to *imagine* + *ary*.

core.definition: A name in Isaiah and Matthew meaning God with us, given to the child whose birth is a sign and used for Jesus as God present with his people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, MAN. The 'yoo' sound is a single syllable, and the last syllable is a reduced 'el'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, religious, and reverent in Christian contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Immanuel as a personal name in Christian families and as a title for Jesus at Christmas and in hymns. In church, saying 'Immanuel' is natural and reverent. It is less common in secular settings, where people would simply say Jesus or the child's name.

distinctions.note: Emmanuel is a common spelling variant, especially in English and French, but Immanuel is the form in the RSV.

examples.everyday: At Christmas our church sings about Immanuel, God with us.
examples.professional: In my sermon I explained why Matthew calls Jesus Immanuel to show his connection to Isaiah 7.
examples.analytical: Matthew's citation of Isaiah 7:14 identifies Jesus as Immanuel, showing God's presence in the person of Christ.

nuance.analogy: Immanuel is like a name tag that says God is here with you.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Immanuel, God is with us, from im, with, plus nu, us, plus El, God.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'IM-uh-nyoo-el'.
Confusing Immanuel with Emmanuel, which is a common spelling variant, and not treating them as different words in the RSV.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name Immanu-El means God with us, from im, with, nu, us, and El, God. Isaiah 7:14 promises a sign that a young woman will bear a son called Immanuel. Isaiah 8:8 uses the name again in a prophecy of the land belonging to Immanuel. Matthew 1:23 quotes Isaiah 7:14 and applies the name to Jesus, the child born of the Virgin Mary.

senses.definition: The quality of being imperious.

core.definition: The quality of being arrogant, bossy, and expecting others to obey without question.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on PEER. Say the ending '-ness' as a reduced 'nuhs', and keep the r clear in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a proud, commanding manner that others find off-putting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'imperiousness' in formal or literary writing, such as a review or character analysis. In speech, they would usually describe the behavior directly, such as 'he's so bossy' or 'she acts like she's in charge of everything.' The noun is rare in everyday life.

distinctions.note: 'Arrogance' is a common word for an inflated sense of self-importance; 'imperiousness' focuses on commanding others rather than on pride alone.
'Bossiness' is casual and everyday; 'imperiousness' is formal and suggests a more lofty, commanding attitude.

examples.everyday: Her imperiousness at the picnic annoyed everyone, since she kept telling us where to sit.
examples.professional: Her imperiousness in client meetings alienated the team, even though her ideas were strong.
examples.analytical: The essay traces the imperiousness of the ruling class to a belief in their divinely granted authority.

nuance.analogy: Imperiousness is like a thick, cold fog that spreads over a room, making everyone feel they must speak quietly and obey.
nuance.etymology: From imperious plus the English noun suffix '-ness', from Latin imperiosus meaning commanding.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'imperialism', which refers to national domination rather than personal manner.
Using it as a common everyday word where 'bossiness' would sound more natural.

senses.definition: Strongly affected, especially favorably.
senses.example: I was impressed with the cleanliness of the hotel.

senses.definition: Stamped, under pressure.
Compelled to serve in a military force.
Confiscated by force or authority.

core.definition: Strongly affected in a favorable way; feeling admiration or respect because of someone's skill, effort, or qualities.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, and the ending is a sharp 'st' with no extra vowel. Many learners add an 'uh' sound before the final t.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it expresses genuine admiration and is a warm reply to good work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I'm impressed' or 'Very impressed' as a friendly compliment in everyday talk, often with a tone of surprise. A natural reply is 'Thanks, I worked hard on it.' The word can also mean stamped, but in daily speech the admiration sense is far more common.

distinctions.note: Impressed describes how someone feels; impressive describes the thing that causes the feeling. 'I am impressed' is a reaction, while 'It is impressive' is a judgment.
Amazed is stronger and expresses surprise or wonder; impressed is milder and usually expresses approval.

examples.everyday: I'm really impressed with how quickly you fixed the sink, Mike; I would have called a plumber.
examples.professional: The hiring manager was impressed with her debugging skills during the technical interview.
examples.analytical: Readers were impressed by the author's argument, yet few of them examined whether its premises could bear the weight placed upon them.

nuance.analogy: Being impressed is like a seal leaving its mark in soft wax: something from outside has left a clear, lasting trace on you.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of impress, from Latin imprimere 'to press into.'
common_mistakes: Using 'impressed' for the thing that causes the feeling; say 'The concert was impressive,' not 'The concert was impressed.'
Using 'impressed of' instead of 'impressed by' or 'impressed with.'

conversation.text: I'm impressed! You cooked all of this yourself?
The interviewer seemed really impressed with her experience.
Honestly, I wasn't that impressed with the new phone.

senses.definition: Pertaining to or characterized by impressionism.
Based on subjective reactions or feelings; not systematically researched or arrived at.
Based on impression rather than reason or fact; based on trying to impress somebody rather than trying for accuracy.
Impressible.

core.definition: Based on general feelings or personal impressions rather than on careful analysis or facts; also relating to the art movement of impressionism.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on NIS, with a lighter secondary stress on PRESH. The 'sion' sounds like 'shun' and the final 'ic' is 'ik.'

nuance.connotation: Often negative in analysis or business, suggesting vague judgment; neutral or positive when describing an art style or a vivid, atmospheric description.
nuance.usage_note: In American professional and academic talk, calling an analysis 'impressionistic' is a polite criticism that it lacks data or rigor. In art and literature, it describes Impressionist painting or writing that captures light and mood. Be careful, because it can sound dismissive if used about a colleague's work.

distinctions.note: Subjective means based on personal opinion, which may be fine; impressionistic implies a looser, less systematic judgment that lacks evidence.
Anecdotal refers to evidence from individual stories; impressionistic describes an overall vague sense, not necessarily a specific story.

examples.everyday: My sister gave an impressionistic description of the new restaurant, something about the lighting and the music, but no details about the food.
examples.professional: Your churn analysis is too impressionistic; we need the actual retention numbers before we present it to leadership.
examples.analytical: Many early theories of religious experience were impressionistic, relying on the author's feelings rather than on careful comparison of testimonies.

nuance.analogy: An impressionistic analysis is like a sketch made from memory: it captures the mood quickly, but it lacks the exact measurements.
nuance.etymology: From impressionism, from French impression 'impression,' plus the suffix -istic.
common_mistakes: Using it as a neutral synonym for 'detailed' or 'vivid' in serious analysis; it usually signals a lack of rigor.
Confusing it with 'impressive,' which praises rather than criticizes.

senses.definition: A doctor or hospital that your health insurance has an agreement with, so you pay less.

core.definition: Describing a doctor, hospital or provider that has a contract with your health insurance plan, so your costs are lower.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NET, with a lighter stress on WORK. Americans say the r in 'work' clearly, though the word ends in a soft, reduced vowel sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals savings, and a good question to ask before a visit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask 'Is Dr. Lee in-network?' before booking an appointment, and the phrase is common on insurance websites and in phone calls with insurers. It is used as an adjective before a noun, as in 'an in-network hospital,' and it is written with a hyphen. A natural reply is 'Yes, she's in-network with Blue Cross,' or 'No, you'll pay more out of pocket.'

distinctions.note: Out-of-network providers have no agreement with your plan, so you usually pay more or the plan may not cover them.
Covered means the plan pays for a service, while in-network describes the provider's contract status, which affects cost.
A preferred provider is a specific type of in-network provider that offers reduced rates, often under a PPO plan.

examples.everyday: Before we book the urgent care, can you check whether they're in-network with our plan?
examples.professional: Our benefits team confirmed that the imaging center is in-network, so the claim should process at the lower rate.
examples.analytical: Insurance networks create a bargaining structure in which in-network status changes both the price a patient pays and the provider's negotiated revenue.

nuance.analogy: It is like a store on a shopping mall's member list: members get the discount there, and others pay full price.
nuance.etymology: 'In-network' combines the English preposition 'in' with 'network,' from Middle English 'net' and 'work,' meaning an interconnected system.
common_mistakes: Dropping the hyphen when using it before a noun, as in 'an in network doctor.'
Assuming in-network means fully covered, when deductibles and co-pays may still apply.

conversation.text: Make sure the doctor is in-network, or it'll cost a lot more.
Is this lab in-network for my plan?
I found an in-network dentist close to my office.

senses.definition: Emitting light as a result of being heated.
Shining very brightly.
Showing intense emotion, as of a performance, etc.
senses.example: The incandescent performance enraptured the audience.

senses.definition: Extremely angry; furious.
senses.example: She is incandescent with rage because someone stole her wallet.

senses.definition: An incandescent lamp or bulb.

core.definition: Glowing with light produced by heat; or extremely bright, brilliant, or emotionally intense.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DES, the third syllable. The final '-ent' is reduced to 'unt'. Avoid saying 'in-can-DES-ent' with a full vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical contexts, positive or intense in descriptive use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'incandescent' with light bulbs, lamps and heated metal, and in describing brilliant anger or joy. You might hear 'incandescent with rage' in a news story or novel. In everyday talk, 'bright' or 'furious' is more common. 'Incandescent rage' is a strong, dramatic phrase.

distinctions.note: 'Luminous' means full of light, often softly; 'incandescent' suggests light produced by intense heat or strong emotion.
'Fluorescent' describes light produced by a chemical or electrical process, not heat.

examples.everyday: Our old house still has incandescent bulbs in the hallway, which get really hot.
examples.professional: The team leader was incandescent with frustration after the outage hit the release.
examples.analytical: The poem's incandescent imagery turns grief into a kind of illumination.

nuance.analogy: Like a filament in an old light bulb: it shines because it is very hot.
nuance.etymology: From Latin incandescere, 'to glow white', from in- plus candescere, 'to begin to glow'.
common_mistakes: Using 'incandescent' as a noun for any light; the noun use means an incandescent lamp only.
Confusing it with 'fluorescent', which refers to a different kind of light.

incandescent.etymology: French *incandescent*, from Latin *incandescens*, from *incandesco* (“be heated, glow”), from *in-* + *candesco*, from *candidus* (“white”).

senses.definition: Without pause or stop; not ending, especially to the point of annoyance.
senses.example: The dog's incessant barking kept the girl awake all night.

core.definition: Continuing without pause or stop, often in an annoying way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, SES. The final -ant is reduced to uhnt, so do not stress it or say it as 'ant'.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, suggesting something tiresome that will not stop, such as noise or complaints.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use incessant for things that irritate, like the incessant barking of a dog or incessant emails. Praising something as incessant sounds odd. In casual conversation people often say nonstop or constant instead.

distinctions.note: Constant is neutral and general; incessant adds the sense of being tiresome or endless.
Continual means repeated with breaks; incessant means with no breaks at all.

examples.everyday: The incessant beeping of the smoke alarm drove us crazy until we finally changed the battery.
examples.professional: Her inbox filled with incessant status update requests, so she turned off notifications for an hour.
examples.analytical: Pascal argues that human restlessness is an incessant motion that distracts us from confronting our mortality.

nuance.analogy: Like a faucet that never fully shuts off, an incessant problem wears you down by never stopping.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin incessans, from in- 'not' and cessare 'to cease'.
common_mistakes: Using incessant for good things, such as 'incessant kindness', which sounds unnatural to most Americans.
Stressing the final syllable; the stress is on SES in in-SES-uhnt.

incessant.etymology: From Late Middle English *incessaunte*, from Late Latin *incessāns*, from Latin *in-* + *cessāns*.

senses.definition: In an incisive manner.

core.definition: In a way that is sharp, clear and direct, cutting straight to the central point of an issue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SY, and keep the final -ly light, as lee. The middle syllable -sive is a short i sound, not a long one.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises precise, sharp expression. It is rarely used in negative contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use incisively in written reviews, academic discussion, and professional feedback, often after verbs like argue, analyze, or question. In casual speech it sounds stiff, so people usually say sharply or really well. It is more natural in print than in conversation.

distinctions.note: Sharply is everyday and can mean suddenly or harshly. Incisively specifically means with clear, penetrating insight.
Astutely stresses shrewd judgment and cleverness. Incisively stresses cutting directly to the central point.
Thoroughly means completely and in depth. Incisively can be brief but very precise.

examples.everyday: My sister explained the problem so incisively that I finally understood it.
examples.professional: She reviewed the proposal incisively, pointing out the two assumptions that could break the forecast.
examples.analytical: Hume argues incisively that causation cannot be directly observed, only inferred from repeated experience.

nuance.analogy: Writing incisively is like slicing a tomato with a very sharp knife: the cut is clean and goes straight through.
nuance.etymology: From incisive plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Latin incidere, to cut into.
common_mistakes: Placing the stress on the first syllable.
Using incisively as if it means simply quickly.
Overusing it in casual speech, where it sounds overly formal.

senses.definition: Too implausible to be credible; beyond belief.
Amazing; astonishing; awe-inspiring.
senses.example: He was so wrapped up in watching the incredible special effects that he couldn't keep track of the story.

senses.definition: Marvellous; profoundly affecting; wonderful; excellent.
senses.example: I had such an incredible slice of pizza last night that I simply can't think about anything else.

core.definition: Amazing or wonderful, so good or impressive that it is hard to believe; also, too unlikely to be believed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KRED, and the -ible ending is a reduced schwa plus l. Learners often stress the last syllable or pronounce the final vowel fully, as in -ibble.

nuance.connotation: Positive in everyday speech, where it expresses enthusiasm; in formal writing it means implausible, which is usually negative.
nuance.usage_note: In casual American conversation, incredible is an enthusiastic word for something excellent, such as a meal, a view or a performance, and people say it often. In a formal or written context it can mean too implausible to believe, so check the context. A natural reply to praise is Thanks, or I know, right?

distinctions.note: Amazing is the more everyday and neutral word for something surprising and impressive, while incredible can add a stronger sense of disbelief.
Unbelievable can be positive or negative, while incredible in everyday speech is almost always positive.

examples.everyday: That pizza was incredible, so we're definitely coming back here.
examples.professional: The team's latency numbers dropped by half, which is incredible for a single sprint.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the miracle narrative is incredible to a modern reader, since its claims seem too implausible to be credible without strong evidence.

nuance.analogy: An incredible result is like a mountain view so clear that you cannot quite believe your eyes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin incredibilis, from in- (not) and credibilis (believable), from credere (to believe).
common_mistakes: Confusing incredible (amazing) with incredulous (unable to believe).
Stressing the final syllable, as in in-kred-uh-BULL.

incredible.etymology: From Middle English *incredible*, from Latin *incrēdibilis* (“that cannot be believed”), from *in-* (“not”) + *crēdibilis* (“worthy of belief”), from *crēdō* (“believe”), equivalent to *in-* + *credible*.

conversation.text: The food at that little taco truck is incredible.
It's incredible how fast the kids grow up.
"We saw a whale from the boat!" "That's incredible!"

senses.definition: In an indelible manner.

core.definition: In a way that cannot be removed, erased, or forgotten.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'DEL', the second syllable. The -ly ending is a light 'blee', and the middle vowel is reduced to 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; often used for lasting marks or memories, which may be positive or negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this to describe something permanently marked or remembered, often in writing or storytelling. It appears in everyday talk too: 'that moment is indelibly printed in my mind'. In casual speech people might say 'I'll never forget it', which is more natural in speech.

distinctions.note: Permanently is neutral and common; indelibly suggests a lasting mark or memory that is hard to forget.
Forever is informal and emotional; indelibly is more precise and often used with verbs like 'marked' or 'printed'.

examples.everyday: That summer at my grandparents' farm is indelibly printed in my memory, with the smell of hay and all.
examples.professional: The incident indelibly changed how our team thinks about backups, and nobody forgets the lesson now.
examples.analytical: The essay shows how colonial history indelibly shapes the language of modern political claims.

nuance.analogy: Like a photograph developed on film: once it is fixed, the image cannot be washed away.
nuance.etymology: From indelible plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Latin indelebilis.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable in 'IN-del-ib-ly'.
Confusing 'indelibly' with 'indelible' used as a noun; here it is only an adverb.

senses.definition: Unfaithfulness in a marriage or an intimate (sexual or romantic) relationship: practice or instance of having a sexual or romantic affair with someone other than one's spouse, without the consent of the spouse.
Unfaithfulness in some other moral obligation.

core.definition: Being unfaithful to a spouse or partner by having a secret sexual or romantic relationship with someone else.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -DEL-, the third syllable. The middle and final syllables are reduced, and the t in the final syllable is flapped, sounding like a soft 'd'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes a serious betrayal in a relationship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use infidelity to talk about cheating on a spouse or partner, in news, counseling, and conversations about relationships. In casual speech people more often say 'cheating'. The word can also mean breaking any serious obligation, but that use is less common.

distinctions.note: Cheating is casual and direct, while infidelity is more formal and used in discussions of relationships or law.
Unfaithfulness is a general term for not being loyal, while infidelity usually refers specifically to sexual or romantic betrayal.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's marriage fell apart after her husband's infidelity, and she is still rebuilding.
examples.professional: HR cannot comment on the rumor of infidelity, because it is a private matter and not part of any company policy.
examples.analytical: Many moral philosophers distinguish infidelity as a breach of promise from other forms of betrayal, because it violates an agreement freely made.

nuance.analogy: Infidelity is like a broken lock on a shared door: the trust that kept the house secure is damaged, even if nothing else looks different.
nuance.etymology: From Latin infidelitas, 'unbelief or unfaithfulness', from infidelis.
common_mistakes: Using infidelity to mean a religious unbelief in modern speech, which is now unusual.
Saying 'infidelity to my friend' for a casual broken promise; it sounds too dramatic.

infidelity.etymology: From Middle English *infidelite*, from Middle French *infidelité* and its etymon Latin *īnfidēlitās*.

senses.definition: A fallacy whose error cannot be represented by the symbols used in formal logic.

core.definition: An error in reasoning that arises from the content or wording of an argument, not from its formal structure.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on FOR in 'informal' and on FAL in 'fallacy'. In American speech 'informal' has the weak vowel in the last syllable, and 'fallacy' has a clear 'uh' before the final -see.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a technical term used in logic, philosophy and argument analysis.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use informal fallacy in philosophy, logic and critical thinking classes, and in debate or academic writing. Outside of those settings, people usually say 'faulty reasoning' or 'a logical error'. It is a precise term, so it works best when you are naming a specific type of error.

distinctions.note: A formal fallacy is an error in the logical structure of an argument that can be shown with symbols, while an informal fallacy depends on the meaning or wording of the claims.
A sophism is a deliberately deceptive argument, while an informal fallacy may be an honest mistake in reasoning.

examples.everyday: When my uncle said everyone agrees with him, so he must be right, I told him that was a common informal fallacy.
examples.professional: In the review, we flagged an informal fallacy in the dashboard summary, because the chart implied causation from correlation.
examples.analytical: The argument commits an informal fallacy of ambiguity, since the term 'natural' shifts meaning between its two premises.

nuance.analogy: An informal fallacy is like a cracked brick in an otherwise well-built wall; the structure looks sound, but the weak spot is in the material.
nuance.etymology: Informal from in- 'not' plus formal; fallacy from Latin fallacia, 'deceit, trick', from fallere, 'to deceive'.
common_mistakes: Confusing informal fallacy with formal fallacy; the difference is whether the error can be shown with symbols.
Stressing 'in-FOR-mal' as in-for-MAL; the main stress is on FOR in American speech.

senses.definition: To make an inquiry or an investigation.
senses.example: Police are already inquiring into the incident.

core.definition: To ask for information about something, often politely or formally, such as asking about prices, hours or availability.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, 'kwire', and the final r is pronounced in American English. Avoid turning it into 'in-QUIRE-ee' or adding a syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it sounds polite and businesslike.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use inquire mostly in customer service, emails and polite questions, such as calling a store to inquire about hours. In casual talk people usually say ask or check, so inquire can sound a bit stiff among friends. A natural reply to a phone call is simply 'Sure, what would you like to know?'

distinctions.note: Ask is the everyday word and works in almost every situation, while inquire is more formal and suits written or polite requests.
To inquire means to ask for information, while to investigate means to examine something systematically to find the facts.

examples.everyday: I called the bakery to inquire about whether they have gluten-free bread on Saturdays.
examples.professional: Please inquire with the vendor about the revised delivery date before our Thursday meeting.
examples.analytical: A careful philosopher must inquire into the assumptions that make a moral claim seem self-evident.

nuance.analogy: Like knocking gently on a door to see who is home, rather than barging in.
nuance.etymology: From Latin inquirere, to search into, from in- and quaerere, to seek.
common_mistakes: Using 'inquire for' instead of 'inquire about' or 'inquire into'.
Confusing inquire with enquire, which is a British spelling variant; Americans spell it inquire.

inquire.etymology: From Latin *inquīrō* (“to seek for”), composed of *in-* (“in, at, on; into”) + *quaerō* (“to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic **kʷaizeō*, from Proto-Indo-European **kʷeh₂-* (“to acquire”).

senses.definition: In an intentional manner; on purpose.

core.definition: On purpose, deliberately, not by accident.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TEN and reduce the other syllables. The 'tion' sounds like 'shun', and the final 'ly' is a light 'lee'. Avoid adding an extra 'tay' sound in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is often used when someone wants to clarify that an action was not an accident, which can sound either reassuring or accusing depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'intentionally' in everyday conversation and at work, often to clear up a misunderstanding: 'I didn't intentionally leave you out of the email.' It is more formal than 'on purpose', so in casual talk people often say 'on purpose' or 'by accident'. It usually comes before the verb: 'She intentionally ignored me.'

distinctions.note: 'On purpose' is the everyday phrase and sounds more casual, while 'intentionally' is more formal and precise.
'Deliberately' emphasizes careful planning, while 'intentionally' only means the person meant to do it.

examples.everyday: I didn't intentionally spill your coffee, so please don't be mad at me.
examples.professional: The API change was intentionally backward-incompatible, so the migration guide covers it.
examples.analytical: The author intentionally leaves the ending open, which forces the reader to decide what the story means.

nuance.analogy: Think of a light switch that someone flips on purpose versus a bulb that flickers by itself. 'Intentionally' describes the switch being flipped.
nuance.etymology: From 'intentional' plus the adverb suffix -ly, from Latin intendere, 'to stretch toward'.
common_mistakes: Placing 'intentionally' awkwardly, as in 'He did it intentionally' is fine, but 'He intentionally did not come' can be unclear without context.
Confusing 'intentionally' with 'intensely' because both are pronounced with similar stress.

core.definition: In the Bible, the name given to Jacob after he wrestled with God; later the name of his descendants, the twelve tribes, and the northern kingdom.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, IZ-. The middle 'ree' is a long 'ee', and the ending is a reduced 'ul'. Do not pronounce the final 'el' as a full 'ell'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in religious contexts; politically charged when used for the modern state of Israel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Israel for the modern state and for the biblical people and land, and context shows which. In Bible study, the name points to the covenant people. In daily conversation about current affairs, the same word refers to the modern state, so be clear about which sense you mean.

distinctions.note: Israel is the name of the nation or the patriarch; an Israelite is one member of that people.
Jew is a later name for a member of the descendants of Judah and the people of Judah; Israel refers to the whole covenant people in the Bible.

examples.everyday: At our small group last night, someone asked why Genesis calls Jacob Israel, and we spent an hour on it.
examples.professional: In the sermon series I explained that the name Israel refers first to a person before it refers to a nation.
examples.analytical: The narrative identity of Israel in Genesis 32 is inseparable from Jacob's struggle at the Jabbok, which names him as one who strives with God.

nuance.analogy: Like a family name given after a turning point in life, which then comes to name the whole family line.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Yisra'el, traditionally explained as 'he strives with God' or 'God strives', from sarah, 'to strive, contend', and El, 'God'.
common_mistakes: Using Israel for the people when you mean the modern state, or the reverse, without clarity.
Pronouncing the name with a stress on the second syllable, as in 'iz-RAY-el'.
nuance.biblical_note: Israel (Hebrew Yisra'el) is first the name God gives to Jacob, and then the name of his descendants, the twelve tribes, the nation under David and Solomon, and the northern kingdom after the division. Genesis 32:22-32 tells of Jacob wrestling at the Jabbok and receiving the new name, which explains the meaning as one who strives with God. Genesis 32:28 records the naming itself. 1 Kings 12:16-20 describes the division of Solomon's kingdom, after which the northern tribes are called Israel. Romans 9:6 distinguishes the children of physical descent from the true Israel of promise.

senses.definition: Saying the forecast predicts rain.

core.definition: Said when a weather forecast predicts rain later today or tonight, though the prediction is not certain.

pronunciation.tip: Stress POHZD in supposed and RAYN in rain. The d in supposed is silent in speech, so it sounds like suh-POHZD, and the t in later is flapped to LAY-der.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is useful information that may change plans.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this to family, friends and coworkers when planning outings, commutes or events. Supposed to means the forecast predicts rain, not that rain is guaranteed. A natural reply is Oh, then I'll grab an umbrella.

distinctions.note: It's going to rain sounds more certain, while it's supposed to rain reports a forecast.
There's a chance of rain gives a probability, while it's supposed to rain states the expected outcome.

examples.everyday: We should bring jackets, because it's supposed to rain later.
examples.professional: Our site visit is outdoors, but it's supposed to rain later, so let's move it indoors.
examples.analytical: The phrase supposed to rain shows forecast uncertainty, since the claim is probabilistic but worded as an expectation.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather app's promise: a reasonable expectation, but not a guarantee.
nuance.etymology: Suppose comes from Old French supposer, from Latin supponere, meaning to put under; rain comes from Old English regnian.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing supposed as suh-POH-sed; the ending sounds like z.
Dropping the 's in it's, which makes the sentence sound like it supposed to rain.

conversation.text: Take an umbrella; it's supposed to rain later.
It's supposed to rain later, so let's enjoy the sun now.

core.definition: A Hebrew name of several men in the Bible, including a priest and a Levite overseer in the post-exilic period, and a temple gatekeeper in the Chronicles genealogies.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, HAN, and the final syllables are reduced to a weak schwa. Do not pronounce the h in the middle as a separate sound; it is a soft breath.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a proper name with no positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter this name mainly in Bible study, sermons, and academic commentary. It is a personal name, so it is written with a capital letter and used without an article. In church settings, people often say the shorter form Johanan, which the Revised Standard Version uses in some passages.

distinctions.note: Johanan is a shorter form of the same Hebrew name, and English Bibles often use it in place of Jehohanan. Both refer to the same Hebrew root.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group got stuck on a list of names, and someone asked who Jehohanan was.
examples.professional: In the seminar handout, we listed Jehohanan among the post-exilic priests to show how the family lines were recorded.
examples.analytical: The genealogical record places Jehohanan within a priestly lineage, and his inclusion signals the community's concern for legitimate temple descent.

nuance.analogy: Like a name on a family tree that shows which branch a person belongs to.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Yəhōḥānān, meaning 'Yahweh has been gracious'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (JEH-o-hanan) instead of the third syllable.
Confusing Jehohanan with Jehoiachin or Jehoiada, which are different people and names.
nuance.biblical_note: Jehohanan appears as a name in the Old Testament, most often in Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah, where several men share the name. The Hebrew Yəhōḥānān combines the divine name with the root ḥānan, 'to be gracious'. Readers should check the context to tell which Jehohanan is meant.

senses.definition: To turn thread or yarn into a piece of fabric by forming loops that are pulled through each other. This can be done by hand with needles or by machine.
senses.example: to knit a stocking

senses.definition: To create a stitch by pulling the working yarn through an existing stitch from back to front.
senses.example: Stitches that are knitted look like little V’s when seen from the front.

senses.definition: To join closely and firmly together.
senses.example: The fight for survival knitted the men closely together.

senses.definition: To become closely and firmly joined; become compacted.
To grow together.
senses.example: All those seedlings knitted into a kaleidoscopic border.

senses.definition: To combine from various elements.
senses.example: The witness knitted together his testimony from contradictory pieces of hearsay.

senses.definition: To heal following a fracture.
senses.example: I’ll go skiing again after my bones knit.

senses.definition: To form into a knot, or into knots; to tie together, as cord; to fasten by tying.
To draw together; to contract into wrinkles.
A knitted garment.
A session of knitting.

core.definition: To make cloth or a garment by looping yarn with two needles or a machine. Also, to join closely together.

pronunciation.tip: The k is silent, so begin with n. The vowel is a short i, as in 'sit,' and the word ends with a sharp t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and warm. Knitting is a common hobby, and to knit people together suggests closeness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly knit as a hobby, and a knitting circle or group is a familiar social activity. To knit people together is a common figurative phrase, often used for families, communities, or teams. Note that 'knitted' and 'knit' are both used as past tense forms.

distinctions.note: Crochet uses one hook to form loops. Knitting uses two or more needles to form stitches that stay on the needles.
Sewing joins pieces of fabric with thread. Knitting creates fabric directly from yarn.

examples.everyday: My grandmother knit me a warm scarf for the winter.
examples.professional: The design team knit together quickly after the reorganization, and the handoffs became much smoother.
examples.analytical: The author argues that shared rituals knit communities together more durably than formal rules do.

nuance.analogy: Knitting is like weaving a rope from loops: each stitch holds the next, and the whole thing becomes firm.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cnyttan, meaning to tie or bind in knots.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the k sound at the start.
Using 'knitted' and 'knit' interchangeably in all contexts; 'knit' is common for the verb, while 'knitted' is typical in adjective uses like 'a knitted hat.'
nuance.biblical_note: In Psalm 139:13 the psalmist says God knit him together in his mother's womb, using a verb that describes forming a body in close and intricate detail. The Hebrew verb is sakak, meaning to cover or weave together. Job 10:11 uses similar imagery, describing God clothing a person with skin and flesh and knitting him together with bones and sinews.

senses.definition: Of a person, following the letter of the law.
senses.example: He's very legalistic, so let's hope the law is just and merciful as well as strict.

senses.definition: Of a person, tending to resort to the law, as one who sues frequently.
senses.example: His legalistic tendencies irritated his neighbors, especially since they had to defend themselves against his frivolous suits.

senses.definition: Practicing or characterized by legalism.
senses.example: She was legalistic in her observation of religious rules and traditions.

core.definition: Following rules or laws strictly, often focusing on the letter of the rule rather than its purpose or spirit.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LIS, the third syllable. Don't stress the first syllable, and keep the middle syllables short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it usually criticizes someone for rigidity or for missing the point of a rule.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use legalistic to criticize a person or organization that follows rules too rigidly, such as a manager who refuses any exception. It can also describe a legal argument that is technically correct but misses the purpose. It is not a compliment, so use it carefully when talking about colleagues or in religious discussions.

distinctions.note: Legal means permitted by law, while legalistic means overly attached to the letter of the law, often in an unhelpful way.
Lawful is neutral and formal about conformity to law, while legalistic is critical of rigid or technical adherence.

examples.everyday: My landlord was so legalistic about the lease that he wouldn't even let us move the couch to fix the stairs.
examples.professional: The compliance team took a legalistic view of the policy, so nobody could get a simple answer about the new process.
examples.analytical: Paul's critics in the letter to the Galatians often read the law legalistically, treating observance as the basis of righteousness rather than as a response to grace.

nuance.analogy: A legalistic reading is like a recipe followed so exactly that the cook forgets what the dish is supposed to taste like.
nuance.etymology: From legal plus the suffix -istic, 'characterized by'.
common_mistakes: Using legalistic as a neutral synonym for legal: legalistic usually implies rigidity or criticism.
Confusing legalistic with legalist in speech: legalistic is the adjective, legalist is the noun for a person.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament the Greek word nomos, 'law', often refers to the Jewish law, and legalism describes an approach that treats keeping the law as a means of earning God's favor. Paul's letters, especially Galatians, argue that righteousness comes through faith rather than the works of the law. Jesus also criticizes those who keep rules while neglecting justice and mercy, as in Matthew 23:23 in the RSV.

core.definition: A place in Judah where Samson killed a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone; also a Book of Mormon prophet, not a biblical figure.

pronunciation.tip: Two syllables with stress on the first. The long 'ee' is followed by a clear 'hye', like the word 'high', and not 'LEH-hy'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name used in religious study and discussion, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Lehi in Bible study and church settings, often with a reference such as 'Lehi in Judges 15'. People from Utah may think first of the city of Lehi, and Latter-day Saint readers know Lehi as a prophet in the Book of Mormon. Clarify which one you mean.

distinctions.note: The Book of Mormon prophet Lehi is not a figure in the Bible; do not confuse him with the place in Judges 15.

collocations: jawbone of an ass at Lehi

examples.everyday: Did you know Samson fought the Philistines at a place called Lehi?
examples.professional: In my sermon I'll explain why the name Lehi is tied to the jawbone Samson used there.
examples.analytical: The name Lehi in Judges 15 links Samson's victory with the Hebrew word for jawbone, creating a deliberate wordplay in the narrative.

nuance.analogy: Like a town named after a famous battle, so that the name itself recalls the event.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew lehi, 'jawbone' or 'cheek', the name tied to the Judges 15 story.
common_mistakes: Confusing the biblical place Lehi with the Book of Mormon prophet of the same name.
Pronouncing the first vowel as short; the first syllable is a long 'ee'.
nuance.biblical_note: Lehi (Hebrew Lehi, meaning 'jawbone') is a place in Judah in Judges 15. Judges 15:9 says the Philistines encamped in Judah and spread out in Lehi. Samson fights there with the jawbone of a donkey (Judges 15:15), and in Judges 15:19 God splits the hollow place in Lehi so that water flows out for Samson to drink.

senses.definition: To make loose.
senses.example: to loosen a knot; to loosen one's grip / hold on something

senses.definition: To become loose.
senses.example: I noticed that my seatbelt had gradually loosened during the journey.

senses.definition: To disengage (a device that restrains).
To become unfastened or undone.
To free from restraint; to set at liberty.
To relieve (the bowels) from constipation; to promote defecation.

core.definition: To make something less tight or less tied, or to become less tight; to release a firm grip or connection.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a light n with no vowel after the s, so say LOO-sn, and do not pronounce a z as in lose.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be literal (loosen a bolt) or figurative (loosen the rules), and it suggests easing tension.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use loosen for physical things like a belt, a jar lid, or a screw, and for easing rules or restrictions. A common casual request is Can you loosen this lid for me? Loosen up is the more casual form used for relaxing.

distinctions.note: Loosen means making something less tight, and the object may stay attached; untie means undoing a knot or rope completely.
Release means let go or set free, often suddenly; loosen is gradual and partial.

examples.everyday: This jar is stuck, so I'll run it under hot water to loosen the lid.
examples.professional: We need to loosen the approval process for small changes so the team can ship faster.
examples.analytical: Some scholars argue that the strict doctrinal boundaries of the early church loosened over time as local communities adapted them.

nuance.analogy: Like loosening a knot: you give the rope more slack little by little until it stops pulling tight.
nuance.etymology: From loose (Old English lēas, free, unbound) plus the verb suffix -en, meaning to make loose.
common_mistakes: Confusing loosen with lose: lose (to misplace or fail) ends in a z sound, while loosen has an s.
Saying loosen up the belt in ordinary speech; say loosen your belt, and reserve loosen up for relaxing.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is lyō, meaning to loose or untie. In Matthew 16:19 Jesus promises Peter the keys of the kingdom and says whatever he binds or looses on earth will be bound or loosed in heaven. In John 11:44 Jesus tells those present to unbind Lazarus, who has come out of the tomb, and let him go, showing loosing as freedom from bondage.

senses.definition: In a loud manner; at a high volume.
senses.example: He spoke loudly so that his brother could hear him from across the street.

senses.definition: In a loud manner; gaudily, showily.
senses.example: to dress loudly

core.definition: In a way that makes a lot of noise or can be heard clearly from far away; at a high volume.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ly is a short, light 'lee', and the l in 'loud' is clear in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes volume, but it can suggest rudeness or embarrassment when someone speaks loudly in a quiet place.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use loudly in everyday speech, often to tell someone to speak more quietly or to describe a noisy situation. In casual talk, people often say 'really loud' or 'turn it up' rather than loudly. Loudly can also be used figuratively for bright or showy things, though this is less common.

distinctions.note: Loud is an adjective and an informal adverb in American speech, while loudly is the more standard adverb form.
Noisily focuses on making a lot of noise in general, while loudly focuses on volume.

examples.everyday: Could you talk a little less loudly? The baby is sleeping.
examples.professional: Please speak loudly enough for the people on the phone to hear you during the meeting.
examples.analytical: The author argues loudly that the institution has ignored the voices of its most vulnerable members.

nuance.analogy: Loudly is like turning a radio knob all the way up until the sound fills the entire room.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hlūd (loud) plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using loud as an adverb in formal writing, where loudly is preferred.
Dropping the final -ly sound and saying 'loud' when speaking carefully.

senses.definition: The act or process of becoming manifest.
senses.example: The last known manifestation of the ghost was over ten years ago.

senses.definition: The embodiment of an intangible, or variable thing.
senses.example: This particular manifestation resembled a young girl crying.

senses.definition: The symptoms or observable conditions which are seen as a result of some disease.
A pattern or logo on a sheet of glass, as decoration or to prevent people from accidentally walking into it.
Willing something into existence (See manifest (verb)).
senses.example: I don't believe in manifestation.

senses.definition: (dated) A political demonstration or protest.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A visible sign or expression of something that is otherwise hidden or abstract, or a symptom of a condition.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on TAY, with a lighter stress on MAN. Pronounce 'tion' as 'shun' and do not give the 'i' a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can describe positive or negative things, depending on what is being shown.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'manifestation' in formal talk and writing, and in medicine when describing symptoms. In casual conversation, they often say 'sign', 'sign of', or 'way it shows up'. In spiritual or New Age contexts, 'manifest' means to bring something into reality through intention, which can sound unscientific in a technical setting.

distinctions.note: A sign is a simple indicator, while a manifestation is a fuller, more visible expression of something deeper.
Symptom is specifically a medical indicator of disease, while manifestation can be general or non-medical.

examples.everyday: Her grumpiness this morning was a manifestation of how little sleep she got.
examples.professional: The system's slow response times are a manifestation of a memory leak in the database layer.
examples.analytical: In Aquinas's account, the created world is a manifestation of divine goodness, though it is not identical with God.

nuance.analogy: A manifestation is like smoke rising from a hidden fire: you cannot see the fire itself, but you see its clear sign.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'manifestare', to make clear or reveal, from 'manifestus'.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the stress as 'man-ih-FES-tay-shun' with the stress on the wrong syllable.
Using 'manifestation' for a simple small sign in casual talk, where 'sign' is more natural.

manifestation.etymology: From Middle English *manifestacion*, *manyfestacion*, *manyfestacioun*; from Late Latin *manifestātiō*.

senses.definition: A noticeable personal habit, a verbal or other (often, but not necessarily unconscious) habitual behavior peculiar to an individual.
Exaggerated or affected style in art, speech, or other behavior.

In literature, an ostentatious and unnatural style of the second half of the sixteenth century. In the contemporary criticism, described as a negation of the classicist equilibrium, pre-Baroque, and deforming expressiveness.
In fine art, a style that is inspired by previous models, aiming to reproduce subjects in an expressive language.

core.definition: A distinctive personal habit of speech or movement, or an exaggerated, affected style in art or behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the -ism ending is a reduced zum sound. Do not pronounce the r as a tapped or rolled sound; use a clear American r in ri.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing a harmless personal habit; negative when describing an affected or excessive style.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mannerism for quirks people have, such as touching their glasses when they think, and for exaggerated styles in art or acting. In casual talk, people say habit or quirk. The capitalized Mannerism is an art-historical period of the late sixteenth century.

distinctions.note: A habit is any regular behavior; a mannerism is more noticeable, often a visible or verbal quirk that marks a person.
A quirk is charming and minor; a mannerism can be charming or can suggest affectation.

examples.everyday: My dad has this funny mannerism of tapping his fingers when he's thinking.
examples.professional: During the interview, I noticed a mannerism of the candidate, a habit of repeating key phrases, that made her answers memorable.
examples.analytical: Many critics treat the painter's elongated figures as a mannerism, a deliberate stylization that departs from classical naturalism.

nuance.analogy: A mannerism is like a signature on a painting: small, repeated, and personal enough that you recognize the artist from it.
nuance.etymology: From manner plus the suffix -ism, a practice or characteristic.
common_mistakes: Using mannerism for a single action; it usually refers to a repeated habit or style.
Stressing the last syllable (man-ur-IZ-um) instead of the first.

senses.definition: A metamorphic rock of crystalline limestone.
A small ball used in games, originally of marble but now usually of glass or ceramic.
Statues made from marble.
senses.example: The Elgin Marbles were originally part of the temple of the Parthenon.

senses.definition: The marbling in meat.
senses.example: The marble is graded using the Australian system.

senses.definition: To cause (something to have) the streaked or swirled appearance of certain types of marble, for example by mixing viscous ingredients incompletely, or by applying paint or other colorants unevenly.
To get or have the streaked or swirled appearance of certain types of marble, for example due to the incomplete mixing of viscous ingredients, or the uneven application of paint or other colorants.
To cause meat, usually beef, pork, or lamb, to be interlaced with fat so that its appearance resembles that of marble.
To become interlaced with fat; to interlace through meat.
To lace or be laced throughout.
Made of, or resembling, marble.
senses.example: a marble mantel

senses.definition: Cold; hard; unfeeling.
senses.example: a marble heart

core.definition: A hard metamorphic rock, usually white or colored with veins, used for statues, buildings, and countertops.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a syllabic l with no vowel, so say it as two syllables, not three. Americans often make the r clearly audible, unlike many British speakers.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. As a material, it suggests elegance and permanence. As an adjective used figuratively for cold, hard, or unfeeling, it is negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use marble for the stone in ordinary speech, such as marble countertops or a marble lobby. The children's game with small balls is usually called marbles, and it is almost always plural in that sense. Calling someone marbled in the figurative sense is rare, so use marble-faced or cold instead.

distinctions.note: Granite is a harder igneous rock with a speckled look, while marble is a softer metamorphic rock that polishes to a smooth, glossy surface.
Limestone is the sedimentary parent rock, while marble is the metamorphosed form that has recrystallized under heat and pressure.

examples.everyday: We put marble countertops in the kitchen last spring, and they look great.
examples.professional: The lobby renovation quote includes marble flooring, so please check the budget before we approve it.
examples.analytical: Michelangelo's David was carved from a single block of marble, and the stone's grain shaped the sculptor's choices.

nuance.analogy: Marble is like a rock that has been reshaped by heat and pressure, the way a hard ideal can be reshaped by time and experience.
nuance.etymology: From Old French marbre, from Latin marmor, from Greek marmaros, meaning shining stone.
common_mistakes: Saying it with three syllables, as mar-uh-ble.
Using marbles (plural) for the stone, when marble is usually singular for the material.
Confusing it with marbled, the adjective for streaked meat or paper.
nuance.biblical_note: Marble appears in Scripture as a costly building and decorative stone. Hebrew shayish (שַׁיִשׁ) names a white, polished stone used in royal palaces, as in the pillars of the Persian court in Esther 1:6. In Revelation 18:12, marble is listed among the luxury goods traded by the merchants of Babylon, symbolizing the wealth and excess of an empire.

marble.etymology: Middle English *marble*, *marbre*; from Anglo-Norman and Old French *marbre*, from Latin *marmor*, from Ancient Greek *μάρμαρος*, perhaps related to *μαρμάρεος* (“gleaming”).

senses.definition: Unbranded.
Showing independence in thoughts or actions.
senses.example: He made a maverick decision. She is such a maverick person.

senses.definition: An unbranded range animal.
Anything dishonestly obtained.
One who is unconventional or does not abide by rules.
senses.example: Among historians he was a maverick because of his belief that history is meaningless.

senses.definition: One who creates or uses controversial or unconventional ideas or practices.
A queen and a jack as a starting hand in Texas hold ’em.
A person in the military who became an officer by going to college while on active duty as an enlisted person.
To take an unbranded range animal.
To seize without a legal claim.

core.definition: A person who thinks and acts independently, refusing to follow the usual rules or group opinions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa, and the 'r' is clear in American speech, making the final syllable sound like 'rick'.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive or admiring, suggesting courage and independence; it can be mildly negative if the person is seen as unreliable or disruptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'maverick' often in politics, business, and sports, to praise someone who breaks from the group. It is common in everyday speech and news. Calling someone a maverick is usually a compliment, although a team or party may use it to describe someone who refuses to cooperate.

distinctions.note: A rebel actively opposes authority, while a maverick may simply act independently without a political aim.
'Nonconformist' is more formal and neutral, while 'maverick' is informal and often admiring.

examples.everyday: My brother is a real maverick; he quit his job to open his own bakery.
examples.professional: She's a maverick engineer who ignores the official roadmap when she thinks it's wrong.
examples.analytical: Kant's ethics is a maverick position within the Enlightenment, rejecting both pure empiricism and simple utilitarian calculation.

nuance.analogy: A maverick is like a calf that wanders off from the herd and refuses to be branded with the herd's mark.
nuance.etymology: Named after Samuel Maverick, a Texas rancher who did not brand his cattle in the 1850s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as in 'may' instead of the short 'a' of 'mav'.
Using 'maverick' for a criminal or fraud; the word means independent, not dishonest.

maverick.etymology: (1803–1870), who refused to brand his cattle.

core.definition: A place in ancient Israel, a watchtower or lookout site where Jacob and Laban made a covenant and where Israel gathered under Samuel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MIZ. The final syllable is a weak uh, and the 'p' is not aspirated strongly. Don't add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a biblical place name with religious significance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often meet Mizpah in Bible study, sermons, and church history. It is a place-name, not a common word, so in conversation you would say 'Mizpah in Genesis' or 'the covenant at Mizpah.' Scholars sometimes write Mizpeh, which is a variant spelling of the same name.

distinctions.note: Mizpeh is a variant spelling used in some translations and Hebrew transliterations; the two words refer to the same name in many contexts.
Mizraim is a name for Egypt and a son of Ham; Mizpah is a place in Israel or Gilead.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group talked about the covenant at Mizpah, where Laban and Jacob made peace.
examples.professional: In the sermon I connected the Mizpah covenant with the idea of God watching over relationships.
examples.analytical: The Genesis account of Mizpah presents the covenant as a witness pillar between two households.

nuance.analogy: Like a border marker that two neighbors set up to remind each other of their agreement.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew miṣpâ, meaning watchtower or lookout.
common_mistakes: Confusing Mizpah with Mizraim, which is an entirely different name.
Stressing the second syllable (miz-PAH) instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew miṣpâ, a watchtower or lookout. In Genesis 31:43-55, Laban and Jacob make a covenant at a heap of stones called Galeed, which is also called Mizpah, and they set up a pillar as a witness. Genesis 31:49 gives the words of blessing, beginning 'The LORD watch between you and me.' In 1 Samuel 7:5-6, Samuel gathers Israel at Mizpah to pray, fast and confess sin before the LORD. In 1 Kings 15:22, King Asa of Judah uses stones from Ramah to fortify Mizpah.

senses.definition: A modest, small, or trifling amount.
senses.example: Unable to garner even a modicum of support for his plan, he conceded to follow the others.

core.definition: A small amount of something, especially of a quality like sense, respect, or comfort that you hope to find.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAH. The middle vowel is a short, reduced ih, and the final syllable is a quick, weak -um.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, since it usually implies that the amount is smaller than you wanted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use modicum mostly in writing and formal speech, often in a phrase like a modicum of respect or a modicum of common sense. Everyday speakers would more often say a little or a bit of. Using it casually can sound a bit stiff, though it is natural in editorials and reviews.

distinctions.note: Bit is casual and everyday; modicum is formal and suggests a minimal amount that you wish were larger.
Iota is even smaller and emphasizes the tiniest possible trace, often in a negative sentence like not an iota.

examples.everyday: The mechanic at the shop had a modicum of honesty, but he still charged me for the extra parts.
examples.professional: The vendor's proposal shows a modicum of attention to our requirements, but it still misses the main performance targets.
examples.analytical: Her argument rests on a modicum of empirical evidence, so its conclusions outrun its premises.

nuance.analogy: A modicum is like the last drop of coffee in a mug: there is something there, but not nearly enough to fill the cup.
nuance.etymology: From Latin modicum, a neuter noun meaning a small quantity, from modicus meaning moderate, from modus meaning measure.
common_mistakes: Using modicum for large amounts; it always implies a small quantity.
Pronouncing it as MOH-dih-kum, which shifts the vowel and sounds unnatural.

modicum.etymology: From Middle English *modicum*, from Latin *modicum* (“a little, a small amount”), a noun use of the neuter form of *modicus* (“moderate; restrained, temperate; reasonable”) + *-cum*.

senses.definition: A commonly served drink consisting of beer and grenadine.
An informal dance competition, where contestants in one quarter of the floor are eliminated by a randomly drawn card representing the corner.

core.definition: A simulation method that uses repeated random sampling to estimate numerical results that are hard to calculate directly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second word, CAR-, and the first word is said MAHN-tee. In General American the vowel in 'Monte' is the same as in 'mon' in the cot-caught merger, so avoid a British 'MON-tay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: In American statistics and science, Monte Carlo is used as a shorthand for Monte Carlo methods, as in 'a Monte Carlo study'. Americans rarely use the name for the casino or the drink and dance senses, which are obscure. In talk, you will hear 'Monte Carlo simulation' more than the bare name.

distinctions.note: Monte Carlo methods simulate data from a specified model; bootstrapping resamples observed data.
An analytical solution gives an exact formula; a Monte Carlo method gives an approximation that improves with more samples.

examples.professional: We ran a Monte Carlo simulation of the forecast with ten thousand scenarios to see how wide the risk range really was.
examples.analytical: A Monte Carlo estimate converges to the true expectation as the number of samples grows, although the rate depends on the variance of the sampled quantity.

nuance.analogy: Rolling dice thousands of times to estimate the odds of a rare outcome, rather than calculating them by hand.
nuance.etymology: Named after the Monte Carlo casino district in Monaco, by analogy with games of chance.
common_mistakes: Saying MON-tay CAR-lo, which is a British-style pronunciation; use MAHN-tee KAR-loh.
Assuming it refers to a casino or a drink in American technical talk; in statistics it refers to the method.

senses.definition: The observation that tasks easy for people, like perception and movement, are hard for AI, while tasks hard for people, like chess, are comparatively easy.

core.definition: The observation that machines find easy human skills, like seeing and moving, hard, but find hard human skills, like chess, relatively easy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MOR in Moravec and on PAIR in paradox. In "paradox," the final syllable is "-dox" with an "aw" sound like "dócks" in General American; the second syllable is weak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical observation used to describe AI limitations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans in AI, robotics, and data science use this name to discuss why perception and motor control are harder for machines than abstract reasoning. The name refers to the roboticist Hans Moravec. It is almost never used outside technical or academic contexts.

distinctions.note: Polanyi's paradox is the idea that people know more than they can say; Moravec's paradox is specifically about machine difficulty with physical perception and motor skills.
The AI effect means people stop calling a task intelligent once machines can do it; Moravec's paradox explains why some tasks are hard for machines to begin with.

collocations: a classic example of Moravec's paradox

examples.everyday: My kid asked why the robot vacuum can clean the whole house but can't pick up a sock, and I told him it's a bit like Moravec's paradox.
examples.professional: Our robotics team keeps running into Moravec's paradox: the language model is strong, but the arm struggles to grasp a cup.
examples.analytical: Moravec's paradox suggests that sensorimotor skills, shaped by hundreds of millions of years of evolution, are harder to reverse-engineer than formal reasoning.

nuance.analogy: It is like a calculator that solves calculus instantly but cannot tie a shoelace, while a toddler does the reverse.
nuance.etymology: Named after the roboticist Hans Moravec, who described the pattern in the 1980s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing Moravec with the stress on the last syllable; the stress falls on MOR.
Confusing the paradox with the claim that AI is generally weak; it specifically concerns which tasks are hard.

conversation.text: Moravec's paradox notes that high-level reasoning is relatively easy for computers, while basic perception and motor skills are hard.
Folding laundry is still a hard robotics problem, which is Moravec's paradox in action.

senses.definition: A feeling of illness or discomfort in the digestive system, usually characterized by a strong urge to vomit.
senses.example: He got nausea after two hours of traveling on the plane.

senses.definition: Strong dislike or disgust.
Motion sickness.

core.definition: An unsettled, queasy feeling in the stomach that makes you feel like you might vomit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, NAW. The -sea ending sounds like 'zee', not 'see', and the final syllable is a reduced 'uh'. Many speakers also say 'NAW-zhuh' in casual speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an unpleasant physical state, so it is usually used when you are describing symptoms or illness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nausea as a medical or everyday word for sick-to-your-stomach feelings, as in 'I have nausea and a headache.' In casual speech people more often say 'I feel sick to my stomach' or 'I feel queasy.' In medical settings, nausea is often paired with vomiting.

distinctions.note: Nausea is the feeling of needing to vomit; vomiting is the act of throwing up.
Disgust is a strong emotional reaction to something unpleasant, while nausea is physical, though the two can overlap.

examples.everyday: I've had a lot of nausea since lunch, so I think I'll skip the spicy food tonight.
examples.professional: The clinic asked me to report any nausea or dizziness after the new medication.
examples.analytical: Descartes treats nausea as a sign that the mind and body are not always reliable witnesses to each other.

nuance.analogy: Nausea is like the warning light on a car dashboard: it is not the breakdown itself, but it signals that something is wrong underneath.
nuance.etymology: From Greek nausea, from naus (ship), because seasickness was the classic example.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am nausea'; use nauseous or nauseated for the feeling.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'see-uh'; it is 'zee-uh'.

nausea.etymology: From Middle English *nausea*, a borrowing from Latin *nausea*, from Ancient Greek *ναυσία* (“sea-sickness”), from *ναῦς* (“ship”), from Proto-Indo-European **neh₂-*.

conversation.text: The medicine can cause nausea, so take it with food.
A cup of ginger tea really helps with nausea.
I had some nausea on the boat, but it went away.

senses.definition: The theory, practice and technology of charting a course for a road vehicle, ship, aircraft, or spaceship.
senses.example: An ocean-going yachtsman must be competent at night navigation

senses.definition: Traffic or travel by vessel, especially commercial shipping.
A canal; a waterway comprising one or more canals and river stretches in communication with one another.
senses.example: the Schuylkill Navigation

senses.definition: The act of accessing different components of the user interface of software.
The process of finding a way through a difficult situation.

core.definition: The process of finding and following a route, especially using maps, GPS, or other tools.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on the -GAY- syllable, and the first syllable has a light secondary stress. The ending -tion is pronounced 'shun'. Many learners stress the first syllable, which sounds unnatural to Americans.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical activity, often with technology, and it is not emotionally loaded.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, navigation most often refers to driving directions and GPS, as in 'the navigation in my car is broken.' It can also mean the field of finding your way on a ship or aircraft. The canal or waterway sense in dictionaries is old-fashioned or mainly British, so Americans would say canal, waterway, or channel.

distinctions.note: Directions are the instructions you follow, while navigation is the process or system that produces and guides them.
Shipping refers to transporting goods by sea or road, while navigation is the art and technology of steering a route.

examples.everyday: Turn on the navigation before we leave, because I don't know the way to the airport.
examples.professional: The new mobile app improves navigation for users who are trying to find their saved orders.
examples.analytical: Early navigation depended on the stars and on sailors' memory, which made the sea a form of knowledge as much as a place.

nuance.analogy: Navigation is like a GPS voice in your head: it keeps telling you where you are and what turn to take next.
nuance.etymology: From Latin navigatio, from navigare (to sail), from navis (ship) plus agere (to drive).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (NAV-ih-gay-shun); the main stress is on GAY.
Using navigation for a canal in everyday American speech; say canal or waterway.

navigation.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *navigation*, from Latin *nāvigātiōnem*, accusative singular of *nāvigātiō* (“sailing, navigation”), from *nāvigō* (“sail”).

conversation.text: The navigation in the rental car is outdated, so use your phone.
The navigation app keeps telling me to make a U-turn.
Turn on navigation; I don't know this part of town.

core.definition: The great river of northeast Africa, flowing north through Egypt to the Mediterranean; in the Bible, Egypt's life-giving river.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, pronounced like the word 'nile' rhyming with 'mile' or 'smile'. Non-native speakers sometimes add a vowel or pronounce it 'NEE-lay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a geographical feature and carries positive associations of fertility and ancient civilization.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the Nile' with the article, as in 'the Nile River', though 'the Nile' alone is standard. It appears in history, geography, and Bible study, and in Sunday school people often mention Moses and the baby in the reeds.

distinctions.note: Nilotic is the adjective and also refers to peoples of the Nile region, such as the Nilotic languages; Nile is the river itself.

examples.everyday: We took a cruise down the Nile when we visited Egypt last spring.
examples.professional: Our geography unit on river systems used the Nile as the main case study for seasonal flooding.
examples.analytical: In Exodus the Nile is both the instrument of Egypt's oppression and the setting of Israel's deliverance, which makes its waters a sign of divine judgment and mercy.

nuance.analogy: The Nile is like a city's main water main: everything in Egypt depended on its steady flow.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Nilus, from Greek Neilos; the ultimate origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'the' before Nile in speech, as in 'I visited Nile', which sounds unnatural.
Pronouncing it as two syllables, like 'NEE-lay'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is y'or (Hebrew yĕʾōr), meaning river or channel, and in Exodus it usually refers to the Nile. In Exodus 1:22 Pharaoh orders that every newborn Hebrew boy be thrown into the Nile, showing the river as a place of threat. In Exodus 7:20 the Nile turns to blood as the first plague, showing the power of the God of Israel over Egypt's chief source of life.

senses.definition: The cardinal number immediately following ninety-one and preceding ninety-three.

core.definition: The cardinal number 92, the one that comes after ninety-one and before ninety-three.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of ninety, NINE-tee, and say the t as a quick flap so it sounds close to 'dee'. Both words are unstressed-to-stressed in the same pattern, so say the second word lightly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is simply a number with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say and write it as one hyphenated word, 'ninety-two', in most contexts, including ages, prices, scores, and page numbers. In speech, people often say it quickly, so listen for the flapped t and the stress on the first word.

distinctions.note: Ninety-two is cardinal (a quantity, 92 things). Ninety-second is ordinal (the position, 92nd), as in 'the ninety-second page'.
Nineteen is 19 and stresses the second syllable (nine-TEEN). Ninety is 90 and stresses the first (NINE-tee). Check the number before you say it.

examples.everyday: My grandmother just turned ninety-two, and she still drives to church.
examples.professional: The model reached ninety-two percent accuracy on the validation set.
